activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the seeding method, chopped chocolate that is already tempered is stirred into melted chocolate to supply form V crystals for the rest to copy.
story:
Joshua had been peeling shallots for twenty minutes when Mr. Cruz finally waved him over to the marble slab, where a bowl of melted chocolate sat cooling in the restaurant kitchen's warm light.

"Tempering," Mr. Cruz said, and nothing else. He was a man who believed a demonstration outranked a lecture. He poured a ribbon of dark chocolate onto the slab and began working it with a spatula, spreading and gathering, spreading and gathering, until the glossy ribbon dulled to matte. Joshua watched the temperature gauge on the counter, a probe stuck in a reserve bowl, ticking downward.

The problem was that Joshua did not own a marble slab. He'd been honest about this from the start, back when he'd asked for the Saturday shift in the pastry section instead of the line, back when he'd admitted he wanted to learn chocolate before culinary school started in the fall. Mr. Cruz had shrugged, which was neither permission nor refusal. Now the demonstration was ending, the chocolate being scraped back into the bowl, reheated gently, and the slab, that necessary cold smooth surface, remained something Joshua could watch but not take home.

"You could get one," said Noam on break, thumbing through his phone. "They're like forty dollars."

"I owe my dad for the deposit on housing."

"Then litigate it with him. Tell him it's an investment."

"My dad doesn't negotiate. He declares."

Shayne, who worked garde manger and had overheard everything, leaned around the corner with a container of leftovers. "You don't need the slab," Shayne said. "You need the seeding method." She popped the lid and showed him a handful of chopped chocolate, irregular pieces, the kind the restaurant bought by the case. "This stuff is already tempered. It comes shiny, it snaps. You stir it into your melted chocolate and it gives the rest something to copy. Form five crystals."

"Form V," Noam corrected, without looking up.

"Whatever the Romans call it. The melted chocolate copies the chopped stuff. It's like it's teaching itself."

Joshua took the container home that night, after Mr. Cruz said only, "Bring back results, not excuses." His mother's kitchen had a double boiler improvised from two pots, a thermometer borrowed from the neighbor who kept bees, and a silence after ten o'clock that made the whole apartment feel quiescent, waiting for him to either succeed or fail quietly.

He melted the chocolate to the temperature the notebook specified, then let it fall, then began adding the chopped pieces a few at a time, stirring. The first pieces vanished into the warm mass, and he could not tell whether anything was happening at all. Stirring, he thought about his father, who ran a hardware store and thought cooking was a populist scam invented by television, who had nonetheless driven him to the restaurant interview and sat in the car for forty minutes. Both of those things were true at once, the way the chocolate was both melted and, if Shayne was right, quietly organizing itself around the seeds he'd dropped in, one crystal pattern spreading through a mass that looked like nothing from the outside.

He tested it the way Mr. Cruz had shown him: he dipped the tip of a knife and set it on parchment. In temper chocolate sets shiny and snaps cleanly; out of temper it streaks and bends. He waited five minutes, then ten, checking the clock the way he used to check for college acceptance letters.

The knife blade came up with a dark, glass-smooth cap of chocolate. He pressed his thumbnail against the edge and it broke with an audible crack, clean as a zipper, and the broken face showed a surface like polished stone. He did it again with a second knife, because one result could be luck. It snapped again.

On Monday he brought the two knife blades wrapped in parchment, still shiny, and set them on the stainless steel counter in front of Mr. Cruz. Mr. Cruz picked one up, bent it near his ear, listened to the snap, and put it down. He looked at Joshua for a long moment. "Seeded?"

"Seeded."

"Then next week you'll do it twice as much, with half the seeds, and you'll tell me when it stops working." He turned back toward the ovens, then paused. "Shayne's still out there, by the way. She wants her container back."

Shayne was in the break room, and when he handed it over she asked, "Did it snap?"

"Like glass."

"Show me the trick with half the seeds," she said, already pulling on her apron.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
The line outside the community hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Mathis had been standing in it for eleven minutes when Derek found him. Derek had his headphones around his neck and his hands in his pockets, which was how he carried everything that mattered, and he said, "I can't believe you're actually doing this. It's a school levy and a county judge. Nobody's drafted anybody."

"That's not the point," Mathis said, though privately he had woken that morning unsure what the point was. He was eighteen years and six days old, and the ballot in his mind had felt embryonic all week, a position not yet a position: his grandfather's voice on one side, Derek's shrugging arithmetic on the other. His grandfather, who had turned nineteen in 1969, had said only one thing about voting when Mathis visited in September. He had been peeling an apple, not looking up, and he'd said, "You know why they gave it to eighteen-year-olds? The slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Because boys our age could be drafted and sent to Vietnam." Then he'd handed Mathis half the apple and gone to watch the news. Mathis had looked it up that night on Derek's phone in the parking lot, and it had checked out, every word, though he hadn't told Derek he'd needed to check.

Inside, the hall had been arranged like a church basement fundraiser: metal folding chairs, a bake-sale table repurposed for sign-in sheets, and Ms. Müller presiding over the voter roll with a pen she clicked in rhythm. Ms. Müller was the reason Mathis had come at all this morning rather than after class. She lived two doors down from his parents and had knocked on their door in October to say this was her fortieth and final election working the polls, and she wanted to see every eligible eighteen-year-old on her street walk through those doors. She had said it holding a rake, dead leaves in her hair, entirely serious. She wanted it, he understood, more than she wanted almost anything, and he did not know how to weigh a neighbor's fortieth and final election against his own first.

"There he is," she said, and her pen stopped clicking. "Mathis, with one s, 4-teen Colby Road." She ran her finger down the roll, and her finger stopped, and she ran it again. Her mouth, which had been ready for a smile, postponed it.

Derek leaned against the bake-sale table behind them, reading a sample ballot like it was in a foreign vernacular. "There's a write-in line," he said. "You could vote for your grandfather. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote." He said it gently, without mockery, which from Derek was its own kind of event.

"Old enough to be drafted," Mathis said. "That's what the slogan was about. They could send eighteen-year-olds to Vietnam, so eighteen-year-olds got the vote. It's the whole reason the age came down to eighteen." Saying it aloud, in this echoing hall, under the folding American flag on its pole, he heard how it both did and did not answer Derek's question about a school levy and a county judge. Nobody was being drafted in Mathis's year. His grandfather had been old enough for a war and had been given a ballot as a kind of compensation, and Mathis was being given the same ballot for free, which was either the point or the proof that the point had evaporated. He held both thoughts the way Ms. Müller held her pen, and neither one clicked.

"Small problem," Ms. Müller said. She turned the binder so he could see it himself. His name was there, but the registration listed a different street, an apartment number from a form he'd filled out at the DMV in August, before he'd moved back home for his gap semester. "The address doesn't match. You can vote, but it'll be provisional. It gets verified later, counted later, if it's counted at all." She said it plainly, watching his face do whatever it was going to do. Behind him, Derek was already cleared, regular ballot, no questions, the whole transaction taking ninety seconds for the boy who had come only because Mathis had texted him three times.

"Does it still count the same?" Mathis asked. "If it's verified."

"Same," she said. "Eventually."

He took the provisional envelope to the carrel by the window, where the sun had warmed the laminated surface, and he stood there for a long moment with the stub of pencil they'd given him. He thought of his grandfather handing him half an apple, and of Ms. Müller with leaves in her hair, and of Derek voting in ninety seconds, and he understood that he was not going to resolve the argument tonight, probably not ever. What he had instead was a considered position with an unresolved center: the vote had been won by people his age, for reasons that no longer applied, and it was his anyway, and he could choose what to do with that. He filled in the bubble for the levy, filled in the judge, and on the write-in line, after a hesitation, he printed his grandfather's full name, then drew a single line through it, then left the line blank.

He sealed the envelope, which might or might not ever be counted, and carried it back to the table where Derek was waiting with his sticker already on his jacket.

"So yours might not even count," Derek said, "and mine does."

Ms. Müller took the envelope from Mathis with both hands, the way she took rakes and election returns and other serious objects, and slid it into the folder marked Provisional, November. "For my last one," she said, "I'd have liked a cleaner story. But they come how they come."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
Violet had taped all nine of her self-portraits to the wall of the art room and stepped back, and the first honest thought she had was that she was looking at the same girl nine times. Same angle of jaw, same grey hoodie, same careful stare. Ms. Reddy had assigned the portfolio weeks ago: ten artworks around a single theme, plus an artist's statement, due before winter break. Violet's theme was "the self as performance," which had sounded sophisticated when she wrote it on the proposal form and now sounded like an excuse to draw her own face.

"What's that face," said Slade, who had come in to raid the supply cupboard for charcoal and stayed to eat chips on the counter.

"That's the problem. I have one face and nine versions of it."

"There's a word for that," Slade said, brushing salt off his sleeve. "Being boring."

She threw a kneaded eraser at him, which he caught, because Slade caught things as a matter of policy. He examined her wall while chewing, tilting his head at each drawing in turn like a man appraising a fence he'd been hired to demolish. His own portfolio, she knew, was ten paintings of highways at night, and every critique in class, Trinity delivered the same scathing verdict: impressive, but you could not tell whether Slade loved the highways or simply could not think of anything else. Trinity's theme was grief, which meant Trinity won every argument by default.

It was Trinity, in fact, who mentioned the photographs. She arrived for sixth period, set down her bag, and looked at Violet's wall with the expression of someone about to be helpful in a way that would sting. "You know what you should look at," she said. "Cindy Sherman. Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. Seventy black-and-white photographs, all of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies."

"Seventy," Violet said.

"Seventy. Same woman every time, and none of them are the same woman." Trinity shrugged, as if to disclaim the evidence. "She's in the library book on the bottom shelf, the one with the cracked spine."

Violet found the book at lunch instead of eating. She turned the pages slowly, forked pasta going cold beside her, and understood within three photographs what Trinity had been too cool to say outright: the sameness was the point. Sherman's face repeated and the person never did. Each invented character had her own lighting, own posture, own movie that had never existed. Violet had been trying to make ten pictures of herself, which was the one thing guaranteed to fail, because she only had so many selves and all of them wore that hoodie.

The question was what to do about it. That afternoon she began sketching, and here she ran into the second problem, the one she would have to carry into her artist's statement whether she liked it or not. One voice in her head wanted total control: plan all ten characters in advance, the runaway, the widow, the girl detective, each in a different invented film. The other voice, which sounded suspiciously like Ms. Reddy, said that performance discovered by accident was more honest than performance designed, that the planned mask was just a different kind of vanity. She could not make both voices happy at once, and she was not sure she should have to.

She compromised, in the unsatisfying and probably correct way that compromises work. She chose four invented characters deliberately and left six slots open to whatever happened: a drawing of herself the way her mother misremembered her, a print made from a photo Trinity took when Violet wasn't ready, a portrait assembled from things classmates wrote about her on index cards. When Slade saw the index-card one, he said it looked like a police composite of a person who didn't exist, and she put it third in the sequence because it was the first one that made her uncomfortable in a useful way.

Ms. Reddy circulated during Thursday's work period, hands behind her back, and paused at the wall. "Your statement draft," she said. "Where is it." Violet handed over the page, expecting the worst, because the page currently said, in its entirety: "I am interested in the gap between who performs and who watches." Ms. Reddy read it twice, which was either a good sign or a very bad one. "A gap needs two sides," she said finally, and moved on to Slade's highways, leaving Violet to decide for herself what that meant.

She decided it meant the viewer was the tenth artwork. She spent Friday after school taping a mirror where the tenth piece should go, a cheap one from the dollar store with a price sticker she couldn't fully peel off the corner, and beneath it she wrote a card: "Untitled Film Still #10, 2024, black-and-white, dimensions variable." Slade said the mirror was cheating. Trinity said the mirror was the only honest thing on the wall. Both of them, Violet noticed, checked their hair in it before leaving.

The part she could not resolve, and did not try to hide in the final statement, was whether ten selves added up to anything. Maybe a person was just a series of stills from movies no one had made, and maybe that was bleak, and maybe it was the opposite of bleak. She wrote both sentences down, one after the other, and let them sit there contradicting each other, because cutting either one felt like lying. Then she turned off the lights, and the mirror kept the room a moment longer than everything else.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere.
story:
Riley would like it noted, for the record, that he was not the one who chose the longer trail. That had been Arnaud, who had pointed at the map with great confidence and said the lookout was forty minutes away, tops, and Riley, being a generous soul and also not looking at the map, had agreed. An hour and a half later they were still climbing through pines, and Riley had begun to suspect that Arnaud's sense of direction was vestigial, an organ evolution had kept around purely for entertainment.

"I said forty minutes," Arnaud said, "and I meant forty minutes of effort. Elapsed time is a different unit."

"You invented that unit just now."

"Units are invented by whoever needs them," Arnaud said, which was the kind of thing he said, and which Riley planned to bring up at every future opportunity, like a debt.

Abigaelle, meanwhile, had stopped caring about either of them and was eating trail mix with the somnolence of a cat in sunlight. Riley had a quiz the next morning, a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century folded in his back pocket, and a plan: explain the greenhouse effect aloud until it stopped feeling like a religion he'd memorized and started feeling like a thing he understood. Abigaelle had volunteered as audience on the condition that she could heckle.

"Okay," Riley said, unfolding the graph against a tree trunk. "So here's CO2, going up, up, up, like a staircase to a room nobody wants to enter. And the planet's getting warmer, and everyone says it's because of this."

"Everyone says," Abigaelle repeated, chewing. "You sound like a lawyer."

"I sound like a person who wants to be exonerated if I get it wrong. Which I won't." He cleared his throat. "Sunlight comes in, warms the ground, and then the heat just, sort of, bounces back down off the greenhouse gases. Like a mirror."

Abigaelle stopped chewing. Arnaud, up the trail, made a sound like a kettle.

"That's wrong," Abigaelle said.

"It's a mirror made of gas."

"Riley. My phone has one bar and I'm spending it on you." She scrolled, held the screen up. Riley read it twice. The ground, apparently, gave off its heat as infrared radiation, and the greenhouse gases absorbed much of that and re-emitted it in all directions, including back down, which warmed the lower atmosphere. It was not a mirror. A mirror would be too easy. It was more like the gases caught the heat and then threw it every which way, like confetti, and some of that confetti fell back on them.

"So the surface gives off heat as infrared radiation," he said slowly, "and the gases absorb it and re-emit it everywhere, including back down."

"That's the whole fact, yes. You're welcome."

"Re-emit," Arnaud said from above them, with the delight of a man collecting evidence. "Not bounce. Re-emit. Riley said bounce."

"Noted for the record," Riley said. The record, he was aware, was getting long, and it was all against him. Around the next bend they found Ms. Côté, their chemistry teacher, sitting on a rock eating an apple, having passed them somewhere without either boy noticing. She had a way of appearing on trails that Riley found mildly supernatural.

"Greenhouse gases," she said, which was alarming, until Riley realized he had been muttering the words for the last half kilometre. "Re-emission," she added, and went back to her apple.

They reached the lookout at 6:40, which Arnaud declared to be "forty minutes, with time zones," and the valley opened below them, the rock face of the far hill still warm and giving off the day's heat into the evening air. Riley held out his hand above the stone, felt it, and thought: infrared, right now, going up. Some of it would be caught on the way out. He looked at the graph again, at the line rising through the decades, and then at the sky, which was turning the exact pink of the inside of a grapefruit.

"Okay," he said. "One more time, whole thing, no heckling."

"Absolutely not," said Abigaelle.

"Surface gives off heat as infrared radiation," Riley said anyway, talking faster. "Greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, and that warms the lower atmosphere. That's why the graph matters. That's why the whole stupid graph matters."

Arnaud opened his mouth. Riley pointed at him.

"Re-emitted," Riley said. "I know. It re-emits. Say one word about mirrors and I'm taking the short way down, and I know exactly where it is."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
story:
The retake was scheduled for Monday morning, and Lily had until then to learn what she had failed to learn the first time. Ms. Bélanger unlocked the lab after last period and set the answer key from the original test face down on the front bench. "You do it yourself," she said. "I'll check it when you're done. If you copy it, you'll only be lost again in June." Then she went to mark quizzes at her desk by the window, and Lily was alone with a balance, a roll of paper towels, and a problem she had gotten wrong twice.

The question asked how many moles of carbon dioxide would form from 55 grams of propane burned in excess oxygen. On the test she had divided by the wrong molar mass, and by the wrong coefficient too, so that her answer was off not by a little but by a kind of order. She had written the molar mass of propane as 44 grams per mole, which was right, and then divided 55 by 3 anyway, because a 3 appeared somewhere in the balanced equation and had seemed important. She could still see the red circle Ms. Bélanger had drawn around it, not angry, just final.

Kiefer came in without knocking, carrying two cartons of chocolate milk, and put one on her bench. "Ophelie told me you were in here," he said. "She said to tell you the library closes at six." He pulled a stool over and sat on it backwards, which was against lab rules and which Ms. Bélanger allowed because it was after hours. "What's the propane doing?"

"Burning. Supposedly. In excess oxygen." She copied the equation from the textbook and balanced it again, slowly, atom by atom. C3H8 plus five O2 gives three CO2 plus four H2O. She underlined the 3 in front of the CO2. "So one mole of propane makes three moles of carbon dioxide. That's the ratio."

"Which problematizes nothing," Kiefer said, "if you don't know how many moles of propane you started with."

"That's the part I skipped." She wrote 55 grams divided by 44 grams per mole and got 1.25. One and a quarter moles of propane. Multiply by three, and the answer was 3.75 moles of carbon dioxide. She checked it by doing it backwards, multiplying 3.75 by 44 to see whether she could recover something like 55, which was not quite the right check, and she knew it, because the 44 belonged to the propane and the product had its own molar mass. She started over and did the backwards check properly, through the ratio, and it held.

Her phone buzzed on the bench. It was a message from Ophelie, who was babysitting across town and could not come.

"Tell Lily," the message read, "that thing from class today helped me. For the gas questions. One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure. My dad has these storage boxes in the garage and I measured one. If I had a mole of gas at those conditions, I'd need something like eleven of them. I stacked them in the driveway to picture it. A mole of carbon dioxide is 44 grams, by the way. Same as your propane, which is a weird coincidence or maybe not. Good luck. Don't overthink."

Lily read it twice, then held the phone out to Kiefer. He read it and set it down next to the chocolate milk. "Eleven boxes," he said. "That's the part I never believe. There are more molecules in a breath than, like, everything."

"I know. But the boxes are the part that helps me." She took a fresh sheet and wrote the follow-up question she expected on the retake: what volume would the 3.75 moles of carbon dioxide occupy. She wrote 22.4 litres per mole, times 3.75, and got 84 litres, and then, because the conditions had to be the ones stated, she wrote at the end, at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere, and drew a box around it. She was honest enough with herself to know the box was a hedge. If the retake gave the temperature as 25 degrees, she did not know what to do about that, and no one had taught her yet.

Ms. Bélanger came over with the answer key still face down and looked at the sheet. "Where did the 84 come from?" she asked, and Lily explained it: grams to moles through the molar mass, moles to moles through the coefficient, moles to litres through the 22.4. Ms. Bélanger nodded once and turned over the key. Lily's numbers matched, all the way down.

Kiefer opened his chocolate milk and drank half of it in one go. "So Monday you're fine."

"Monday I'm fine if the temperature is zero," Lily said. She stacked her sheets, squared them against the bench, and wrote at the top of the last one, in small letters, ask about 25 degrees. Then she folded it into the back pocket of her binder, next to her grandmother's recipe cards, the only patrimony anyone had left her, which she kept there for no reason she could defend. "I'm going to email her the question tonight," she said. "If she answers before the weekend, I'll practise it. If she doesn't, I'll do the zero-degree problems and hope."

Ms. Bélanger locked the lab behind them. The hallway smelled of floor wax, and the windows at the end of it had gone dark. Lily zipped her bag over the calculator, impermeable to the drizzle that had started while they worked, and Kiefer held the door. "Eleven boxes," he said again, out into the parking lot. "I'm going to measure my dad's too."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
The envelopes had been Samantha's job since November, when her grandmother first pressed the stack of red paper into her hands and told her she was old enough now. Old enough for what, exactly, her grandmother hadn't said, but Samantha understood it as a kind of enfranchisement, an admission into the smaller rooms of family business where money was counted and children were discussed. On the morning of the New Year gathering, she sat at the kitchen table with the bills fanned out in front of her, still crisp from the bank, and folded each one lengthwise the way her grandmother liked.

Her little cousin crouched beside her, seven years old and magnetic in her certainty, stuffing napkins into spare envelopes to imitate the ritual. When Samantha looked up from her arithmetic, the girl had taken two twenties from the pile and was sliding them toward the red paper, intending, apparently, to make her own gift.

"That's forty," Samantha said. "You can't put forty in."

"Why not? Forty is a lot."

"It's a lot with a four in it." Samantha pulled the bills back and replaced them with a fifty. "Give a fifty. Or thirty, thirty's fine. Just not a number with four." The girl frowned at her with the particular suspicion of someone who has caught an adult making rules up on the spot, and Samantha realized she was not entirely sure she could defend the rule if pressed. She had absorbed it the way she had absorbed which dishes went on which altar, without ever being taught it directly.

The house filled by noon. Aunts steamed dumplings in the kitchen while uncles argued about parking, and the smell of scallion oil and citrus drifted through rooms already crowded with shoes at the door. Samantha moved through it with her tray of envelopes, and it was there, in the hallway outside the kitchen, that she handed one to her grandmother's oldest friend and saw her grandmother watching her, waiting, the way one waits for a coin to land.

Later, at the folding table in the back room, her mother sat down across from her and began crimping dumpling edges without ceremony. "You changed the amounts," her mother said. It wasn't a question. Samantha admitted that she had, that she'd redistributed everything so no envelope held a four, not forty, not four itself, nothing with the digit in it anywhere. She had spent twenty minutes on it, cross-checking like a bank teller.

Her mother kept her eyes on the dumplings. "The word for four sounds like the word for death," she said. "That's all it is." Then she pinched another edge shut and let the silence sit between them, because she was a woman who believed explanations should be as brief as surgery.

Samantha had come into the day holding two ideas that had never had to share a room before. At school, in Ms. Mori's class, she had learned to call things like this superstition, to sort them into the column of claims that hadn't earned their keep. Yasser, whose erudition ran to everything and made him insufferable at lunch, would have said the association was arbitrary, a phonetic accident, nothing more. He would have been right. And yet her grandmother's care was not arbitrary. Her grandmother, whose frugality was practically congenital, who reused tea bags and kept rubber bands in a drawer for forty years, had happily paid the difference to move every envelope off the number. What Samantha had first dismissed she now saw could be held at the same time as the skepticism, the way you can know a map is not the territory and still use the map. She didn't know yet whether that was wisdom or just a compromise she could live with, and she was honest enough with herself to leave the question open.

In the evening, after the trays of food had been reduced to glossy remnants and the little cousin had fallen asleep against the arm of the couch with a red envelope still clutched in her fist, Samantha found her grandmother at the kitchen sink washing the good dishes by hand. Samantha picked up a towel and stood beside her, drying each bowl as it was passed over. Neither of them said anything. When the last bowl came across, her grandmother looked at the towel in Samantha's hands, then at her face, and handed her the dish anyway.

"One more for the shelf," her grandmother said. "The high one."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.
story:
The new warm-up arrived in the second week of the season, stapled to the bulletin board of the cinder-block dugout: single-leg squats, Nordic curls, jumping drills, lateral hops over the foul line. Ethan read the sheet twice while lacing his cleats, then read it a third time, because none of it looked like baseball. Fifteen minutes of every practice would now go to it, and the first baseman, a junior named only ever by his nickname, said what most of them were thinking, that if he wanted to hop side to side he would have gone out for volleyball.

Ms. Swampy ran it. She was the neighbour of the athletic director, a retired physiotherapist who had agreed to come to the field twice a week with a stopwatch and a folding chair, and she was neither harsh nor munificent with her praise; she said "better" when a repetition improved and nothing at all when it did not. On the first day she had them land from a low box with their knees over their toes, and she stopped the whole line when Ethan's teammate Bree let her knee collapse inward. "Again," Ms. Swampy said, and Bree did it again, and did it again, until the sun moved a full length along the outfield grass.

The grumbling organized itself by the third week. The catcher, who was the team's best hitter and its laziest conditioner, started a quiet practice of arriving late enough to miss the first block of drills, and by the middle of May half the infield had joined him, stretching on the fence beyond first base while the rest of them hopped and balanced in the dirt between the mound and home. Ethan stayed with the routine, partly because he was eighteen and trying to keep a starting spot in right field, and partly because his left knee had given a soft, unprompted click in April that he had not told anyone about.

He wanted to know what the routine was actually for, and nobody would tell him in a way that satisfied the want. Ms. Swampy offered only corrections. So one Thursday, while the field drained from an afternoon rain and the practice was cut short, he sat on the bench with his phone and searched the words printed at the bottom of the handout. He transcribed one sentence into the notes app, carefully, because he had a habit of getting things almost right: neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. He read it, then read it aloud under his breath near the empty on-deck circle, the vowels flat against the chain-link.

Maliyah, the shortstop, found him there. She had stayed with the routine too, though she complained about it more than anyone, and she asked what he was muttering. He showed her the screen. "It's for the knees," she said, scanning. "Ligaments. So that's why she's obsessive about the landing." Ethan said the part he kept turning over, that the program didn't promise anything, it only reduced a risk, and she shrugged and said that was how everything worked, seatbelts included, and went to collect the bases.

The distinction between reducing a risk and eliminating one occupied him more than he expected. He had grown up, like most of them, inside a rough kind of determinism: do the work and you get the result, slack off and you don't. The routine offended that logic because it paid out invisibly, in injuries that never happened, which was a ledger nobody could read. He tried explaining this to Bree on the bus to the away game at Northgate, and she listened with her chin on her fist and then said, "So I could do every drill and still tear something in June." Ethan said yes. She said, "Great, cheer me up why don't you," and put in her earbuds, though she was smiling a little when she did.

Bree, in fact, was the one who converted the infield. In the first inning at Northgate she broke back on a liner over second, planted to change direction, and came up limping, not injured but shaken, holding the side of her knee and waving off the coach. She played the rest of the game at three-quarters speed. On Monday she was first in line for the hopping drills, ahead even of Ethan, and the catcher, who had watched her limp to the bus, drifted over from the fence without a word being said to him. Within two weeks the whole infield was doing the routine, arriving early for it, and Ms. Swampy began adding a second box.

The click in Ethan's left knee did not come back, or if it did, he missed it. He kept the sentence in his notes app all season and looked at it sometimes on the bench between innings, not because it told him what would happen but because it told him honestly what it could: less risk, never none. On the last Saturday of June, with the season over and the field already booked for a summer league, he stayed after the others had gone and did the drills alone in the settling dark, landing soft, knees over toes, the dirt cool through his cleats. When he finished he stood at the plate and looked out at the outfield fence, at the light going orange above it, and he took one more jump, straight up, and came down easy.

"Not bad," Ms. Swampy said from the folding chair behind the backstop, where she had been sitting the whole time.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
Stella found the guitar behind the shelving in Mr. Augustin's music classroom, leaning in its case like something that had been asked to wait. "It was my uncle's," Mr. Augustin said, not looking up from the worksheets he was marking. "Take it home if you want. It hasn't been tuned since the spring." She carried it to the bus with the case bumping her knee, and at her kitchen table she opened it and plucked the fattest string. The note came out dull and low, lower than the E she knew from piano, and when she pressed her tuner app against the soundhole it told her the string sat somewhere near a D. She had no idea guitars drifted like that, all six of them, quietly, while nobody played.

At school the next day she cornered Marcel in the hallway by the vending machines. "I looked it up," she said, turning her phone toward him. On the screen was a diagram of a guitar neck with letters at the head of each string. "From the lowest string to the highest, it's E, A, D, G, B, and then E again. The same E at both ends, an octave apart." Marcel squinted at it. "So the thin one and the fat one are both E?" "Both E," she said, and the repetition of it pleased her, the way the scale folded back on itself at the top, like a stairway that ends where it began.

She had assumed, before that, that learning an instrument meant memorizing where to put her fingers. Her grandmother had taught her piano that way, drilling scales until Stella could play them disaffected and automatic, her hands moving while her mind was somewhere else entirely. The guitar seemed to want something different from her. It wanted her to listen first. For three evenings she sat on her bed turning the tuning pegs a quarter-turn at a time, hunting for the needle on the app to settle at A, then D, then G, and she began to notice that her ear arrived before the needle did. She could hear the wobble of a string that was almost right, the beating of two pitches arguing with each other, and the tuner became less an authority than an encumbrance she tolerated, a crutch she was already outgrowing.

Marcel watched her tune it in the music classroom on Thursday, his chin on his hand. "How do you know when it's right?" "It stops fighting itself," she said. "A chord that's in tune sounds like one thing instead of six things." Mr. Augustin, shelving reeds at the back, glanced over but said nothing, which Stella had come to understand was his way of approving. She played an E chord, all six strings open in some places and pressed in others, and for the first time the sound came out round and complete, and she laughed before she could stop herself.

That Friday Timothy came in with his own guitar, a glossy electric he'd had for two years, and he tuned by ear in about forty seconds, no app, his head tilted like a bird listening for worms. Stella watched his fingers and felt something complicated: admiration, and underneath it a small hard knot of envy. She had worked for her tuning; he seemed to have been born inside it. "You play long?" she asked. "Since I was nine," he said. "My dad made me practice an hour a day." He shrugged. "I mostly hated it till I didn't."

Later that afternoon, alone in the emptying classroom, Stella sat with the uncle's guitar across her lap and thought about Timothy's shrug. She had spent years believing that talent underpinned everything, that the kids who could just do it were a different species, and that the rest of them were pretending. But her own hands had learned the pegs in three days. Her ear had learned to hear the wobble in one week. And Timothy had hated the hour a day until one day he hadn't, which sounded less like a different species and more like the same species further along the same road. Maybe those two things were both true at once. Maybe some people started ahead, and everyone still had to walk.

She picked out the notes of a song she liked, slowly, hunting for each one, and she noticed that the melody lived inside the tuning, that the E, A, D, G, B, E was not a chore she had finished but a landscape she had just entered. Where would the next note be? She wondered what else was hiding up the neck, past the fifth fret, where Marcel said the same shapes made new chords. She wondered whether her ear would keep improving or whether it would plateau the way her piano playing had, and she couldn't tell yet, and strangely that didn't bother her.

The janitor's cart squeaked past the doorway. Stella checked the fattest string one more time, out of habit now rather than need, and it held its low E, steady and sure. She put her thumb across all six strings and dragged them down, listening, and the whole instrument rang out at once.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Electric field strength can be measured in volts per metre or in newtons per coulomb, and the two units are equivalent.
story:
The physics lab smelled of warm dust and pencil shavings, and Simon had claimed the corner bench because its window caught the last of the afternoon. He set up the two parallel plates with the care of someone who had already broken one that semester, spacing them exactly as the worksheet demanded, and clipped the voltmeter leads to their terminals before Yohan and Grayson arrived arguing, as they so often did, about something neither had actually measured yet.

"It's four thousand," Grayson said, dropping his bag on the stool beside Simon's. "Volts per metre. I did it before lunch."

"Then you did it wrong, because I got four thousand newtons per coulomb," Yohan said. He was already leaning over Simon's shoulder, reading the meter upside down, which he did whenever he was too impatient to walk around the bench. "Those aren't even the same thing. Mine's a force. Yours is just, like, voltage spread out."

"Mine's the field strength," Grayson said. "It says so on the sheet."

Simon, who had learned over three years of shared classes that these two could calcify into an argument the way wet concrete sets if nobody interrupted, put his pencil down. "Same number, though," he said. "Both of you got four thousand."

"That's a coincidence," Yohan said.

"It's not a coincidence if it's the same point between the same plates." Simon tapped the worksheet where he'd marked the point P, six centimetres in, dead centre between the plates. He had his own answer hidden under his forearm, not because he was secretive but because he wanted to watch the meter settle first. The needle eased to two hundred volts, and he wrote it in the margin. "Two hundred volts across fifty millimetres. Go on, divide."

Grayson divided and got four thousand volts per metre. Yohan divided and got, grudgingly, four thousand newtons per coulomb, and then sat back on his stool as if the calculator had personally offended him. "So which one is it actually? They can't both be right. They're different units. A volt isn't a newton."

On the wall above the chalkboard, Mr. Romano had pinned a photograph from some long-ago field trip, a montane ridge above a research station where, the caption said, they had measured atmospheric potential gradients with a field mill. Simon had looked at it a hundred times without ever really seeing it, and now he looked at it again, at the little instrument standing in the thin air, and thought that whatever it read out there, someone had had to decide what units to call it in.

He pulled the textbook toward him, found the reference table in the back, and ran his finger down the column. "Look," he said, and turned it so both of them could see. He didn't read the entry aloud. He let them find the line themselves, the one that listed the two units side by side, unbothered, as though it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

"They're equivalent," Grayson said slowly. "Volts per metre and newtons per coulomb. They're the same unit written two ways."

"Two names for one thing," Yohan said. He said it in the tone of a man discovering he had been fighting over the deed to a house he already co-owned. Then he laughed, short and surprised, and Simon felt something in his own chest loosen too, though he kept his face level because Grayson hated being laughed at, even gently, even when the laugh was mostly at himself.

Grayson was quiet for a moment, turning his pencil between his fingers. Simon watched him decide, watched the decision happen in his shoulders before it reached his mouth. "Fine. I was calling it field strength like the sheet does. You were calling it force per charge. It's both. That's not me being wrong, that's the sheet being boring."

"It's both," Yohan agreed, and then, because he was Yohan, immediately ruined the peace. "But I got there first."

"There's no first," Simon said. "It's not primogeniture. Nobody inherits the right answer." He slid the voltmeter leads across to Yohan, who had left his own in his other bag, the one he always forgot, and Yohan took them without comment, which between them was a kind of thank you. Grayson, meanwhile, had begun sketching the plates again from scratch, more carefully this time, labelling the point P with a small neat arrow.

Simon looked down at his own hidden answer, still under his forearm, and found that he hadn't written the units after the number at all. Four thousand, bare, waiting. He thought about the two ways of seeing the same thing, one rooted in what the charge would feel pushed by, the other in how the potential dropped across the distance, and how both of them were true at once, and how the book hadn't really explained why, only stated it, and he still couldn't have said why himself. He was going to have to sit with that. He uncapped his pen.

"Newtons per coulomb," he said out loud, and wrote it, then added, after a glance at the window where the light was going amber on the glass, "and volts per metre. Both. Write both if you want to be insufferable about it."

Yohan wrote both. Grayson wrote both and underlined them, twice.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
The line outside the council chamber began forming before the folding tables were even steady, and Colton finished taping the last registration sign to the front just as Ms. Oyelaran appeared with a crate of pamphlets. She ran the youth volunteer program at city hall, and today, a Saturday of all days, the county had opened the rotunda for a civic fair: booths for the league of women voters, the county clerk, a mock polling station where anyone could practice filling out a ballot. Colton had signed up mostly because Ocean had, and Ocean had signed up mostly because Amine had threatened to spend the whole day there alone, truculent as ever, arguing with anyone who walked past the constitutional trivia table.

"Ask us anything," Amine announced to a man in a green windbreaker, who did not ask anything and kept walking. Amine was not discouraged. Amine was never discouraged. Colton dragged a second chair over and settled in beside him, and for the first hour the questions were easy ones, where to register, how to change an address, whether the mock ballots counted for anything. They did not, though people lined up for them anyway, drawn by the little "I VOTED (SORT OF)" stickers Ms. Oyelaran had printed at her own expense.

Then a girl from the international school came through, maybe sixteen, lanyard from a model UN conference still around her neck. "Okay, you said ask anything," she said. "So my cousin lives in Spain, and I never get this straight. They have a king. But she's always posting about the prime minister too. Why do some countries have both a king and a prime minister? Who's actually in charge?" She looked at Colton specifically, the way people did when he was the one making eye contact.

Colton opened his mouth and then closed it. He had a folder of notes, because Ms. Oyelaran made every volunteer prepare one, and somewhere in it was a diagram he'd copied from a comparative government textbook three nights ago at his kitchen table. He found the page. "So," he said slowly, watching the diagram as if it might rearrange itself, "a lot of parliamentary systems split it up. The king is the head of state. Ceremonial kind of stuff, ribbon cuttings, being the country's face. And the prime minister is the head of government, the one who actually runs things day to day. Two different jobs, two different people."

"Like a president and a prime minister?" the girl asked.

"It doesn't have to be a king," Colton said, and this part he was proud of, because he'd only learned it Tuesday. "Some of them have a ceremonial president instead of a monarch, but it works the same way. The head of state is separate from the head of government." He tapped the diagram. "Here's the part that got me, though. In the United States, the president is both. Same person, both jobs at once."

The girl frowned at the diagram, then at the mock polling station across the rotunda, where a woman was feeding a practice ballot into a cardboard machine. "Huh," she said. "So when we vote for president, we're kind of voting for two jobs?" Colton said he guessed so, and she took a pamphlet and drifted toward the stickers.

At the lunch break, Ocean flopped onto the stage steps with two slices of pizza and an argument already assembled. "You made it sound like the American way is worse," Ocean said. "Like splitting the jobs up is obviously smarter."

"I didn't say that."

"You said it got you. Your whole thing is that it got you."

Amine leaned back on both elbows, delighted. "It's the trivia table problem. Every answer is right in one frame and wrong in another."

"That's just relativism," Ocean said, "and I don't accept relativism about term limits."

Colton laughed, but the exchange stayed with him through the afternoon, the way a stone stays in a shoe. It wasn't that he thought one system was smarter. It was that the two systems were answering different questions. In a parliamentary system the legislature could pull the prime minister out mid-term, a vote of no confidence, that was the phrase, the whole chamber deciding it had lost faith. In a presidential system the voters chose the head of government directly, on a fixed date, and short of impeachment there was no pulling that person out early, however badly things went. Removal versus election: one put the leash in the hands of parliament, the other in the hands of the ballot and the calendar. He turned this over while restocking pamphlets, and the more he turned it, the less it looked like a ranking and the more it looked like a choice about which risk you preferred to live with.

At four, Ms. Oyelaran collected the leftover stickers and told them they could go, and Amine found Colton still sitting at the table, diagram out, pen in hand. "You're doing homework at a volunteer thing," Amine said. "That's a new low."

Colton pulled out his phone instead, because Ocean had gone quiet an hour ago, which for Ocean meant thinking, and there was a message waiting. "Okay fine," it read. "Maybe you're not ranking them. But answer me this. If the parliament can fire the prime minister whenever, doesn't the head of state matter more than we say? Somebody has to be the country when the government falls apart. Somebody has to be the thing that doesn't fall apart. Also Amine says you're exculpating the textbook and I should ask what that means but I'm not going to. Come outside, we're getting ice cream, last chance."

Colton pocketed the phone and looked once more at the diagram, at the two boxes he'd drawn and the single American box that held both. He still didn't know which he'd choose if choosing were up to him. He folded the page in quarters and put it in his back pocket, where it would ride home soft and creased and still, somehow, unanswered.

"Two scoops," he called, pushing through the rotunda doors into the late sun. "And I'm picking the flavor, Ocean, because you always get the same one."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a black cat peers over Kahlo's shoulder, usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death.
story:
The print had hung in his grandmother's back room for as long as Andrew could remember, between a framed prayer and a photograph of a street in Guanajuato nobody in the family could identify. He had spent whole afternoons under it as a child, drawing at the low table, without once looking up. Now he stood in front of it with his phone, taking notes, because Mr. Wu had assigned a formal critique due Monday and Andrew had left his textbook at school.

"A painting you live with," Mr. Wu had said on Friday, which Andrew had taken as permission. He had a page of vocabulary, a half-formed thesis, and a grandmother who was in the kitchen making him tea he did not want.

Keanna arrived first, laptop under her arm, because she had refused to do the critique alone. Ludovic followed, having texted that he was coming and then, characteristically, arrived an hour later with two energy drinks and no notes at all. They spread out on the carpet of the back room, under the painting, and Andrew's grandmother set down the tea and studied their arrangement with the mild suspicion of a despot reviewing an unfamiliar cabinet of ministers.

"Is that the one with the animals?" Ludovic asked, dropping onto the couch. "Mr. Wu loves the animals."

"There's a monkey," Keanna said, tilting her screen toward the print for comparison. "And a hummingbird. Obviously the hummingbird."

Andrew stood back and tried to see it the way the assignment demanded, as shape and color before meaning. The background was arboreal, a dense green that pushed forward against the figure, so that Kahlo's face seemed both submerged and advancing, and the leaves behind her were darker than the foliage of any actual forest, closer to jade, close to black at the edges. He wrote that down. He wrote down the horizontal of her shoulders, the flat, frontal stare, the way the necklace of thorns pulled the composition into a V that pointed at the hummingbird hanging dead from its throat. Then he stopped writing, because in the upper left of the painting, above her shoulder, two round eyes were looking back at him.

"There's a cat," he said.

"Where?" Keanna came to stand beside him.

"Left side. Peering over her shoulder." He hadn't seen it in years of afternoons under this print, or perhaps he had seen it and filed it away with the wallpaper, another quiet watcher in a house of watchers. His grandmother, he remembered suddenly, had once told him cats knew things, and he had been seven and had believed her completely, and at some point he had stopped believing her without ever deciding to.

Ludovic got up, drink in hand, and squinted. "Okay, so we've got monkey, hummingbird, cat. And dragonflies, or butterflies, something with wings near her hair. So the assignment says symbolism. What's each one doing there?"

"The monkey's hers," Keanna said, scrolling. "It's in a bunch of her paintings. Like a pet, but also like a child, or like a stand-in for her. It's holding the thorn necklace, sort of adjusting it. Almost tender."

"Almost," Andrew said. "It's also the thing keeping the thorns on her."

"Fine, it's ambiguous, that's the whole point of Kahlo," Ludovic said. "The hummingbird, dead, black, hanging where a pendant would go. That one's not ambiguous."

"And the cat?" Keanna asked.

Ludovic drained his can. "Black cats. Bad luck. Death. That's the standard reading, everybody says that."

Andrew looked at the animal longer. It watched her the way it watched everything, unblinking, over the shoulder of a woman who stared straight out at the viewer as if to say she already knew the cat was there and had decided not to turn around. He thought about how much of the painting was organized around what Kahlo would not look at. The cat, the thorns drawing blood at her neck, the dead bird at her chest. She externalizes everything she refuses to face, he wrote, then crossed out refuses, then wrote it again, because the first word was the truer one even if he couldn't yet defend it.

His grandmother came in for the teacups and paused at the print. "That one always watches," she said, nodding at the cat, and went back to the kitchen, and none of them said anything until the door had closed.

For the critique, the trouble was proportion. If every animal was a symbol, the painting became a ledger: monkey equals this, bird equals that, cat equals death, add them up, thesis complete. That was the version Ludovic wanted to draft, and it would probably earn a B. But the assignment had asked for formal analysis first, color, composition, and Andrew kept noticing that the cat's eyes were the same yellow as the half-hidden dragonflies, and that the black of the hummingbird and the black of the cat's body were not the same black at all, one glossy, one flat, as though the two deaths in the painting had different textures. He didn't know what to do with that observation. He wrote it in the margin anyway.

"So what's our position?" Keanna asked, pulling the document toward herself.

"That the painting sets up a readable code and then breaks it," Andrew said slowly. "The animals are symbols. The cat's watching her, and the tradition says that means bad luck and death coming. But the composition won't let you settle on that, because she's looking at us, not at any of it. The symbols are behind her and she's in front of them." He heard how it sounded and added, "I can't prove the second half."

"Then put in the part you can prove and flag the rest," Keanna said. "Mr. Wu says he'd rather see the seam than a fake conclusion."

Ludovic had already stretched out on the couch, eyes half closed, in the exact posture Andrew associated with every group project of the last four years. "Write it," Ludovic said. "I'll read it tomorrow and argue with one sentence so it looks like I contributed."

Andrew pulled the keyboard over. Above him the cat went on peering over the painted shoulder, patient, patient, waiting for someone to turn around.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
The ball left Ewan's hand at a shallow angle, cleared the top of the climbing frame, and landed in the woodchips near the seesaw. Charlotte stood at the throwing line with her phone, timing it. "Two point one seconds," she said.

"Time it again," Kamila said. "You flinched."

She hadn't flinched, but she timed it again anyway, because the whole project depended on the number being right. Mr. Doyle had set the assignment on Friday: verify a calculation with a real throw, bring the measurement to Monday's class. Ewan, who could throw a football in a clean arc and didn't mind standing in the cold, was the thrower. Kamila held the tape measure. Charlotte was supposed to be the one who understood the equations, and she did, mostly, except that she had equivocated all weekend about one step and now the weekend was over.

The second throw hung up a little higher. "Two point two," she said, and wrote it down. "That's the time in the air."

"Is that the one we're using?" Ewan picked up the ball and walked back, breath showing in the air.

"We're using all of them. We need an average." She crouched on the woodchips with her notebook and drew the throwing line, the climbing frame, the landing zone, the seesaw, all to scale. On the page she had split the throw into two directions, the way the textbook did. Vertical, which rose and fell. Horizontal, which just went. The vertical part was where she had spent her weekend, solving for how long the ball stayed up, and it had come out near what her phone was telling her, which was something.

Kamila stretched the tape from the throwing line to the scuffed patch where the second ball had landed. "Nine and a half meters," she said. "Wait, do I measure to where it first hit or where it rolled?"

"First hit. It has to be first hit," Charlotte said, and then, because she heard how quickly she had said it, she added, "That's the honest number. After it bounces we're not tracking anything."

Ewan threw five more times while the light went flat and orange over the roofline of the school across the street. Charlotte timed each one. The times clustered around two point two seconds, tight enough that she stopped holding her breath before each catch of the number. The distances clustered around nine and a half meters, except one that drifted to ten because Ewan leaned forward on the follow-through and Kamila called him on it.

Then she sat on the bottom rung of the climbing frame and did the thing she had been avoiding. If the ball was in the air for two point two seconds, and it covered nine and a half meters sideways in that time, then the horizontal velocity was the distance divided by the time. About four point three meters per second. She checked it against the throwing angle Ewan had roughly maintained, forty degrees, and the speed he claimed he threw at, and the two didn't agree, and she sat with that disagreement for a minute before she saw what it meant. Going the other way worked better. Take the vertical equation, the one she trusted, get the time in the air from it. Then multiply that time by the horizontal velocity, which didn't change during the flight, and you got exactly where the ball would land. Not approximately, not a guess with a margin. The landing point, one multiplication away.

"Say that again," Kamila said, because Charlotte had said it out loud without noticing.

"The time in the air times the constant horizontal velocity gives you the horizontal distance. That's the whole thing. That's how you find where it lands." She turned the notebook around so Kamila could see the arrow she had drawn, one going straight across at even speed, one going up and down. "You don't even need the arc. You need the clock and you need the sideways speed."

"That's it? That's the whole chapter?"

"That's a whole chapter."

Ewan took the ball back to the line. "Then predict one before I throw it. Tell me where it lands."

Charlotte looked at her numbers, then at the woodchips. "Put your bag at nine and a half meters."

He dropped his duffel on the scuffed patch and threw. The ball came off his hand flat, lower than the others, and Charlotte watched it the way she now knew she could, watching the clock in her head while her eyes tracked the sideways drift. The ball cleared the climbing frame, dropped, and hit the dirt a meter short of the bag.

"That's wrong," Ewan said. "You said it lands there."

She checked her timing against the phone. One point eight seconds in the air, not two point two. He had thrown it flatter, angrier, the way a person throws when they're cold and being tested. The rule hadn't failed. The input had changed. She said so, and Kamila laughed, and Ewan insisted he had thrown exactly the same, which he plainly hadn't, and for a moment Charlotte felt the strange vertigo of it: the equation was right and the throw was wrong and both of those things were true at once, and which one you trusted depended on what you were trying to do.

Mr. Doyle came around the corner of the school with his dog, saw the three of them, and slowed. "Monday's assignment," he said. It wasn't a question.

"We can predict where it lands now," Charlotte said. "Give me the time in the air and one multiplication gives me the landing spot."

He looked at her notebook, then at the duffel bag, then at the scuffed woodchips beside it. "Whose injunction was it to measure to the first bounce?"

"Hers," Kamila said.

"She'll do fine." He clipped the leash back on the dog and went on down the path, and Charlotte thought about explaining the flattened throw to Ewan, about how the method held even when the arm didn't, but instead she picked up the ball and tossed it to him.

"Again," she said, holding up the phone. "Same as the first ones this time. Not like you're angry at it."

Ewan wiped his hand on his jacket, squared his feet, and threw.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In Westminster-style parliaments such as the UK's, the second reading is a debate and vote on a bill's general principles, before its details are examined.
story:
The bill had started as one sentence on the whiteboard, and by Thursday it had grown teeth. Addison read it aloud while Ariane leaned over her shoulder, the paper smelling of the toner from the library printer, warm and faintly chemical. "An Act to enfranchise sixteen-year-olds in municipal elections." Josue had wanted to add the word "duly" before "enfranchise," because it sounded official, and Ms. Liu had let them argue about it for a full ten minutes before suggesting, mildly, that they might move on.

The committee stage had been the hardest part. They had sat in a tight circle after school, the room gone amber with low sun, and gone through the bill clause by clause. Josue, who had appointed himself guardian of the preamble, kept returning to the placement of a comma. "If the comma comes after 'municipal,' it changes the scope," he insisted, tapping the page so hard the paper crackled. Ariane rolled a marker back and forth under her palm and said the scope was obvious to anyone with eyes. Addison, chairing only because Ms. Liu had looked at her when no one else volunteered, let them fight until the custodian's vacuum started up in the hallway, a low drone through the door.

She had gone home and, out of stubbornness more than curiosity, looked up how a real parliament did it. She found the answer in a dry procedural guide, its prose almost ascetic, stripped of anything that wasn't rule: readings, stages, divisions. She read the sentence three times, then copied it into the margin of her draft bill in pencil. Second reading: a debate and vote on the bill's general principles, before its details are examined. The details came later, in committee. The comma came later. She hadn't told Josue.

Friday, the debate collapsed inside four minutes. Josue rose with his notes, his voice pitched to fill the room, and immediately began on the comma, its tyranny, its capacity to undo the entire scheme of enfranchisement. Ariane stood to counter him and somehow they arrived at the question of whether "duly" was or was not redundant, and a boy in the second row called out something about semicolons, and Ms. Liu sat at her desk with her hands folded, watching, saying nothing. The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and someone's mango chapstick. Addison could feel the afternoon slipping through her fingers like water.

She stood up. "Point of order." She had never used the phrase before and it came out steadier than she expected, loud enough that Josue actually stopped talking. "We're still on second reading." He blinked at her. "That's the stage where you debate the general principles," she said, "before the details get examined. That's what second reading is. The comma is a detail. The committee already had it for a whole afternoon, and it nearly killed us." A small laugh went around the room, not at Josue exactly, though he flushed. Ariane was grinning.

"So the question in front of the House," Addison went on, her heart working hard now, "is whether this bill's principle is right. Should sixteen-year-olds vote in municipal elections. That's it. That's all we're deciding today."

The debate restarted, and it was different. Josue, once he had recovered, argued that voting was a habit and habits formed early, that a sixteen-year-old who voted once would likely vote forever. Ariane, opposing, said that being able to name a bylaw was not the same as understanding one, that enthusiasm was not competence. Addison listened and took notes, and what she noticed was that both of them were partly right and neither would admit it. She believed sixteen-year-olds should be trusted with a municipal ballot; she also knew Josue, who could not drive yet, had strong opinions about parking policy he had arrived at by vibes. She held both of these observations in her head without letting either one cancel the other, and she wrote in the margin: the principle stands; the voters will be imperfect, like the rest of us.

When the division was called, they voted by standing. Twelve rose for the bill, seven against, one abstention. Ms. Liu recorded it on the board in her looping hand, then declared the bill read a second time and referred it, as she put it, back to committee for clause by clause study, where the comma could have its day. Josue raised both fists as though he had won something. Ariane kicked his chair lightly on her way past, and he caught her ankle before it connected, and for a second they were both almost smiling.

The third reading came Monday, faster, almost ceremonial. The amended bill passed again, the comma now living wherever Josue had finally agreed it should live. Ms. Liu, playing the role of the Crown, took the paper from Addison, read it once, and said, "I hereby signify assent," pressing a rubber stamp onto the bottom corner with a small, decisive thump. The ink was blue and the page was warm from her hands and Addison realized she was holding her school's first law, or the model of one, its edges already soft from passing between so many people.

Ariane found her at the door, coat half on. "You only said that because you'd looked it up," she said. "The second reading thing."

"I looked it up Tuesday. After committee."

"So you sat on it all week."

"I wanted to see if we'd get there ourselves," Addison said. "We didn't." Ariane pulled her scarf tight and looked at the paper still in Addison's hand, the blue stamp shining under the corridor lights. "Do it again next semester," she said. "Pick something harder this time. I want to beat you properly."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
The scoreboard above the shallow end said 6 to 4, and Dorothy had the ball. Eva was open at two meters, treading water with her arm up, but Dorothy spun and fired it instead toward Priya, who had scored three goals in the first half. Priya's shot skidded off the crossbar and into the lane line, and the other team collected it and swam away. "She's hot," Dorothy gasped as they trailed the play. "You pass to the hot hand."

"I was open," Eva said. "I'm always open. That's my whole strategy."

"You're always open because nobody's guarding you, which honestly is information too." Dorothy was grinning, but she kept swimming toward the attacking end, and Eva understood that the argument was suspended, not settled, until the next whistle.

It had started in Mr. Pérez's statistics class, the week before finals, when he'd put a question on the board about coin flips and then said, almost as an aside, that a famous paper had looked at whether streaks were real. Eva had gone home and found it herself: a 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky, which concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance. In the margin of her notebook she'd written, in pen, "the hot hand is a fallacy," and underlined it twice, which was the kind of thing she did when a fact felt like a weapon she could use later. Now the water polo season was in its last fortnight, and she was holding the weapon in a chlorinated pool, and Dorothy refused to believe it existed.

At the interval, Eva dragged herself onto the deck and dripped a puddle around her cleats of information. "Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky," she said, ticking the names off on wet fingers. "Nineteen eighty-five. Basketball shooters, streaks, no more common than chance. It's called the hot hand fallacy."

"You memorized it," Leo said, awed. "That's so sad."

"It's called studying." She flicked water at him. "The point is Priya's three goals don't predict a fourth. You pass to whoever's in position. Position is real. Vibes aren't."

Dorothy wrung out her cap and looked at Eva with something like pity. "Okay, scientist. You know what else is real? Pragmatics. Like, the pragmatics of a team where everyone thinks you've jinxed the best shooter by making her self-conscious with your spreadsheet voice." Priya, overhearing, laughed so hard she had to hold the gutter.

The second half destabilized Eva's certainty faster than she would have liked. Priya scored twice more, both on assists from Dorothy, and Eva's own attempts, taken from position, immaculately selected by probability, rang off the post once and were blocked twice. The nascent feeling that she had understood something about the world curdled slightly into the feeling that the world had understood her, and was teasing her. At 8 to 7 with ninety seconds left, Eva found herself, absurdly, hoping Dorothy would pass to Priya anyway.

What actually happened was that Leo got the ball at half distance, saw Priya doubled, and threw it to Eva, who was, once again, open. She had time to think, in the half second before the defender arrived, that this was exactly what the study would predict and also exactly what she was afraid of, and then she stopped thinking and shot. The ball hit the water inside the post and the horn went and the scoreboard changed to 8 to 8, which was the end, because this league does not play overtime in June.

In the changing room afterward, Dorothy sat on the bench unlacing her cap and did not say anything smug, which was somehow worse. Eva sat down beside her and pulled a sandal out of her bag upside down. "So I still think the study's right," she said. "I just don't know if right wins games."

"Or you don't know if it was right tonight," Dorothy said. "Or Priya's actually hot and the basketball players were just bad at basketball. You said it yourself, one study, one sport, one million years ago."

"Nineteen eighty-five."

"Ancient history." Dorothy stood and shouldered her bag, then paused at the door, dripping, magnanimous in victory or in draw. "Next season I'm passing to you, by the way. You made two in a row at the end of practice Tuesday."

"Statistically that means nothing," Eva said.

"Great," said Dorothy. "Then you'd better shoot anyway."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love.
story:
The projector hummed in the art room while twenty printouts of Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird sat on the long tables like place mats at a very serious dinner. Ms. Berg had assigned each of them a paragraph of formal analysis, due Friday, and had written three words on the board in her cramped, recalcitrant handwriting, the kind that resisted being read from the back row: colour, composition, symbolism. Lucas had chosen the printout nearest him and immediately regretted it, because Jonathon leaned across the aisle and said, "That's the one with the dead bird, right? Easy. Say it symbolizes death, collect your marks, go home."

"That's not how it works," Lucas said, though he was not entirely sure how it worked, which was the problem. He could see the composition well enough. Her face floats dead center, frontal as an icon, the thorn necklace slicing a dark line across her throat, the monkey at one shoulder and the black cat at the other balancing each other like arguments on a scale. Behind her, leaves press in from every edge, green layered on green, so that the figure seems sutured into the foliage rather than placed before it, stitched in like a wound being closed. The blood at her neck was only a few pinpricks of red, and yet his eye kept going back to them, two tiny drops doing more work than the whole expanse of jungle.

"Symbolizes death," Jonathon repeated, as if repetition were analysis. "It's a dead bird, Lucas. Dead birds mean death. That's like the first rule of symbolism."

Ryley, who sat by the window and rarely spoke unless spoken to, looked up from her own printout. "My abuela has one of those," she said. "A hummingbird charm. In a little glass box on her dresser."

Jonathon laughed. "A dead hummingbird? On her dresser?"

"Not dead. A little metal one. But she told me the real ones, the actual birds, people used to hang them like that. She said it's a Mexican folk charm, a dead hummingbird hanging at your throat, for luck in love." Ryley shrugged, embarrassed suddenly, as though she had revealed a family recipe. "I don't know if Kahlo knew that. Probably, though. She was into all that stuff."

The room got quieter than it had been, the specific quiet of twenty people pretending to keep working. Lucas looked at the printout again and the painting rearranged itself. The bird was not a memento mori, not a little feathered skull whispering remember you must die. It was a charm, an appeal, worn at the throat the way a crucifix is worn, and Kahlo had painted herself wearing it the year after her divorce, with thorns biting her neck and blood beading beneath them. Luck in love, purchased with pain. The necklace and the bird were the same argument in two materials, one of suffering and one of hope, and Ms. Berg's three words on the board were suddenly not three assignments but one question.

"It could still mean both," Jonathon said, defensive now, sensing that his easy paragraph had collapsed. "A charm for love that's a dead thing. That's ironic. That's a thing."

"That's actually a fair point," Lucas said, and meant it, which surprised him.
