He had come into the room wanting the right answer, the one that would survive Ms. Berg's red pen, and instead he had found two readings that both held weight, like the monkey and the cat, one pulling toward sweetness and one toward watching and waiting. He could not sut the two together neatly; the charm did not cancel the death, and the death did not mock the charm, or maybe it did, and the honest thing was to write the critique holding both, with the seam visible. When he tried to draft a sentence about what the bird "really meant," his pen stalled. The etiology of his own certainty was unavailable. He did not know, and the paragraph would have to say so, or at least refuse to pretend otherwise.

Ms. Berg drifted past their table on her circuit of the room and paused over Ryley's printout. "Interesting choice," she said, in the tone she used when she meant the opposite of nothing.

"She didn't choose it, I did," Lucas said. "There's a thing about the bird. Ryley's grandmother, the charm, luck in love. It changes the whole composition, the thorns and everything. Or it doesn't change it, it complicates it. I'm still deciding."

Ms. Berg looked at him for a moment longer than teachers usually look, then said, "Undecided is a position, if you hold it on purpose." She moved on toward the supply closet, and Jonathon slid his printout across the aisle until it sat next to Lucas's, the two identical women regarding each other with their small dark eyes and their bleeding necks.

"Fine," Jonathon said. "Say it's a dead bird that means love. Say she's wearing hope like a corpse at her throat and the thorns are the price." He tapped the printout. "But if I get a worse mark than you, you're explaining the etymology of my C to my mother."

"That's not what etiology means," Lucas said, and picked up his pen.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
story:
Carter backed the family hatchback between two wheelie bins for the ninth time that evening, and for the ninth time the rear tire kissed the kerb with a soft, damning thud. Mr. Balogun, who had come out to water his tomatoes and then stayed to watch, made a noise through his teeth like a man watching his team concede.

"You are steering too early," he said from the lawn. "Wait until your shoulder passes the bin, then turn hard."

"I know," Carter said, and immediately heard how petulant it sounded, so he added, "Thanks," which made it worse. He pulled forward and started again, hands at ten and two the way his instructor insisted, though his instructor had also told him to relax, and the two instructions seemed to cancel each other out. In the side mirror the kerb slid closer, a grey ribbon of judgement.

Josie was sitting on the low wall by Mr. Balogun's garage, ostensibly revising, actually scrolling. "Your test is when, Thursday?" she asked. "And you're curbing it the night before. Bold strategy."

"It's one thing. It's a curb." Carter got out and walked around to look at the gap he'd left, which was generous enough to park a bus in. Perfect parking left thirty centimetres, his instructor said, and Carter had apparently interpreted that as a minimum, not a maximum.

"One thing can fail you," Josie said. "My cousin rolled back on a hill start, just a little, and that was it. Six months of lessons, done in one second."

Vera arrived on her bike at that moment, one hand holding her phone like a torch. "Okay, I looked it up," she said, braking hard enough to skid slightly on the gravel. "Because Josie's cousin is, respectfully, a drama queen. On the practical test in Great Britain, you can pass with up to fifteen driving faults. You just can't have any serious or dangerous faults. So a curb touch, if the examiner thinks you were in control, that's a driving fault. You get fifteen of them. Fifteen."

"Fifteen," Carter repeated, as though tasting the word. He tried to imagine accumulating fifteen small mistakes and still being handed a licence. It felt like a grading system designed by someone merciful, or by someone who understood that everyone curbs it sometimes. He was not sure which, and the difference seemed to matter.

"It can't be that generous," Josie said. "That would mean you could stall, miss a mirror, kerb it, indicate late, and still pass."

"Sixteen times you couldn't," Vera said. "Fifteen times you could." She showed them the screen. Carter read it twice, the garage door behind Mr. Balogun's dormant car gleaming with evening light, and something in his shoulders came down half an inch. Then he thought about the word serious and how he wouldn't be the one deciding whether a mistake was serious, and the inch went back up.

"Okay," he said. "Then tomorrow, on the merge, I don't hesitate." He had been hesitating all week on the slip road by the retail park, slowing at the give way line like a coward in an old film, cars stacking behind him. His instructor called it the one habit that could genuinely sink him, because crawling into sixty-mile-an-hour traffic had a way of turning a small error into a large one, into the kind of fault that didn't count toward fifteen because it wasn't that kind of fault at all.

Mr. Balogun set down his watering can. "When I did my test, in Lagos, the examiner took off his hat and put it on the dash. If the hat fell, you failed. Everything else, he said, was conversation." Carter laughed, and even Josie smiled at her shoes. It occurred to Carter that everyone who had ever learned to drive had carried some private theory of how many mistakes a person was allowed, and that the official answer, fifteen and no more, was either a comfort or a dare depending on the day.

On Thursday morning the examiner turned out to be a compact woman with a clipboard and a voice like a satnav. The parallel parking came early, between a van and a silver car, and Carter waited until his shoulder passed the silver car before turning hard, exactly as he'd practised, and the rear tire kissed the kerb anyway, a touch so light he almost pretended not to feel it. He watched the examiner's pen. She wrote something short.

At the slip road he did not hesitate. He looked, signalled, and went, and the car settled into the traffic like a hand into a glove, and for three whole seconds he felt like someone who already knew how to do this. Then the examiner said, "Take the next left and return to the test centre," and he realized he had no idea what she had written, either of the times, and would not know until she added it all up at the end, some mistakes counting, some not, according to rules he had only ever half understood.

He parked in the bay, put on the handbrake, and looked at the clipboard upside down.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime.
story:
The moving truck idled at the curb on Alden Court while Blake carried the last box, the one with his records and his father's old atlas, and noticed that the street had no trees tall enough to shade anything. Back on Marshin Road the maples had dropped seeds every June, and he and Alexis had flicked the spinning ones off the porch rail like small helicopters. Here the saplings were staked and skinny, each one a promise somebody had made to the ground and then left. His mother was taping shut a box of kitchen things that should have been taped an hour ago, and his father was leaning in the truck's open door, reading something on his phone.

"Did you know," his father said, "the Census Bureau did a survey in 2007, and they estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime."

"Eleven point seven," Blake said. "So somebody out there is moving point-seven of a time."

"Somebody out there is packing half a kitchen." His father pocketed the phone and picked up a lamp.

Blake set his box on the porch and sat on it. Eleven point seven. This was move number four for him, which meant, if he let the arithmetic run, seven or eight more awaited him somewhere in the fog ahead, in towns he could not yet picture, with saplings not yet planted. He had always thought of moving as something that happened to his family, a private catastrophe with its own weather, but apparently it was a national average, a thing most people did. That reframed it somehow. He tried to historicize it, the way Mr. Sandhu had taught them in seminar: not "why is this happening to me" but "what conditions make this happen to nearly everyone." Highways. Jobs. Rents. Whole systems of drift that his family was just riding, one small boat among millions.

A girl came up the sidewalk with a dog on a long leash, stopping at every sapling the way people stop at bulletin boards. She wore a lanyard from some summer program, flipped backward. "You're the ones in number twelve," she said. "I'm Faye. Number eight. Did you know they planted these trees the same week everybody moved in? Like the houses and the trees all arrived together."

"So nothing here is older than the moving trucks," Blake said.

"Except the dirt." The dog strained toward a hydrant and she reeled it in. "Where'd you come from?"

"Forty minutes east. Which sounds close, but it's a different school, so it might as well be a different century." He surprised himself with how bitter that came out, and softened it. "My friend Alexis stayed. She's already texting me the parking lot like it's a war memorial."

Faye laughed. "My dad still does that with his hometown gas station. Demolished eleven years ago and he grieves it annually." She looked at the box under him. "What's in there that you're guarding with your whole body?"

He opened the flaps. The atlas, and beneath it the records, and beneath those a shoebox of things Alexis had given him at the going-away party: a spun maple seed she'd lacquered, a ticket stub, a note that just said "eleventh grade syllogism: Blake is miserable in June; June happens every year; therefore." She'd meant it as a joke about the heat. He read it differently now.

"Is that supposed to be logic or an insult?" Faye asked, peering.

"Neither. It's a math nerd saying goodbye." He turned the lacquered seed over in his fingers. Here was the thing he kept circling: if he believed Alexis, then leaving was just another June, a misery on a schedule, congenital to being anybody's kid in a country where 11.7 moves came standard. But if he believed his father's tone, casual as weather, then moving was ordinary and his grief was a rounding error. Both couldn't be fully true, and neither felt entirely false. Maybe the seed was both too: a thing that spun as it fell, and a thing that, given ground, dug in.

"Can I show you something before you finish unpacking?" Faye said. "There's a drainage pond behind the model homes. It's completely unglamorous. There are frogs anyway."

Blake looked back at the truck, at his mother waving a roll of tape like a flag of distress, at the saplings standing in their perfect indifferent row. He put the seed in his pocket, where it made a small ridge against his leg.

"Lead the way," he said. "I want to hear a frog that chose this place."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The transition, or bridge, is the passage in the exposition that modulates from the home key to the second key, and it often uses busier, less tuneful material.
story:
Jesse arrived at Ms. Vu's studio with the score of Mozart's Sonata in B-flat, K. 333, already dog-eared at page two, because he had spent the train ride arguing with himself about where to draw the first pencil line. Ms. Vu, laconic by nature, took the score from him, looked at the three coloured pencils he had lined up on the music stand, and said only, "Mark the exposition. First theme, second theme. Then we'll see."

That was the problem. She would not tell him where anything began.

He played the opening sixteen bars, then the next eight, and stopped with his hand hovering above the page. The tuneful part seemed to end somewhere around bar twenty-three, but then came another tuneful part, and another, and by bar forty he had bracketed four separate "first themes" in faint pencil, crossed out three of them, and heard the metronome ticking on the shelf like an accusation. "You're guessing by vibes," he muttered at himself, and Ms. Vu, watering a peace lily in the corner, did not disagree.

At home that night, Sandrine texted him a photo of her own score, marked up for the same assignment. Her message read: "I put the double bar at 23, then changed it to 41, then ate a whole bag of pretzels about it. My dad says Mozart is just showing off and the themes run into each other on purpose. Do you think Ms. Vu wants us to be wrong? Also did you figure out where the second key starts, because that's where SHE put her bracket when I asked and she just said 'you tell me.' She's literally a menace." Jesse typed back, "Working on it," set the phone face down, and played the exposition again, slower, with his eyes closed.

The second time through, he noticed something he had skated past before. Around bar forty-one, the music stopped singing. The left hand began churning, the right hand ran through figuration that no one would hum on a bus, and underneath it the harmonies leaned away from B-flat, leaning and leaning, until the whole piece had tipped into F major and settled there, and a new melody arrived, sweet and singable, in the new key. He grabbed the score. The passage before the new melody was busier and less tuneful than anything around it, and it was exactly where the key changed.

"Ms. Vu," he said at the next lesson, before his coat was off. "The first theme doesn't end where the tune ends. It ends where the bridge starts. There's this busy part, no real tune, and it modulates from the home key to the second key. That's the transition. That's how I know the first theme is finished." He laid his pencil across bar forty-one like a fence.

Ms. Vu watered nothing this time. She sat down, played the passage with the pedal half down, and let it hang in the air. "The transition," she said. "Or the bridge. Yes."

"Sandrine thought it was twenty-three," Jesse said. "So did I, for two days. I kept falling back into counting bars until the melody stopped, like some kind of recidivism. Wrong method, over and over." He turned the page and bracketed the second theme in F, then the closing section, then, after the double bar, the development, which shattered the themes and wandered through keys like a rumour. The recapitulation, when it came, gave him a new problem: the bridge came back but didn't change key, and he sat with his pencil poised, unsure whether it still counted as a bridge if it went nowhere new.

"Both of those are true," he said finally, writing a question mark in the margin instead of a bracket. "It's a bridge and it isn't. I can't make it one thing."

He played the exposition through from the top, and when he reached the busy passage he lifted his left hand slightly, letting the churning fall quiet, so that Ms. Vu could hear the modulation happen underneath, the floor tilting from B-flat into F. She stopped him at bar fifty with a raised finger.

"Now the second theme," she said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
The festival on Carner Avenue had closed the street to cars and opened it to everything else, which was how Ella found herself carrying her family's menorah through a crowd of strangers eating fried dough. Her mother had gone to find her grandmother near the stage, leaving Ella with the brass menorah wrapped in a dish towel and one instruction: get it to the community table by sundown, and don't drop it, because it had survived four moves and one cat and it was not going to die at a street festival.

She was studying the menorah under a string of lights when Sameer appeared at her elbow, holding a paper boat of latkes he had no intention of sharing. "Is that a candelabra situation?" he said.

"It's a menorah. And I'm counting."

"Counting what?"

"Whether we have enough candles." Tonight was the fourth night. Ella had a box of candles in her coat pocket, and she had been trying, on the walk over, to work out how many she needed, and she had come up with a different answer twice. She'd counted eight branches, then eight again, and then a candle had shifted in the box and she'd lost her place entirely, and now she was standing in front of a crowd of food stalls doing arithmetic on an object she'd seen every winter of her life.

Kamille arrived, stole a latke from Sameer's boat, and forestalled his complaint by pointing. "Look, they have a hanukkiyah at the community table already."

"They're the same thing," Ella said, a little too quickly, and then frowned, because she wasn't entirely sure that was true, and saying things too quickly when she wasn't sure was exactly what her grandmother called her signature move.

The community table sat between the bookstall and the churro cart, which struck Ella as a very honest arrangement: the story of the oil on one side, the hedonism of fried sugar on the other, and nobody pretending the two didn't coexist. Mr. Bighorn, whose roof her father had repaired in the fall and who had showed up in a kippah he looked genuinely pleased about, was arranging candles in the table's menorah. Ella watched him set in the candles one at a time, right to left, and something in her chest untangled.

"Wait," she said. She counted his candles, jabbing a finger at each one. "Five. But it's the fourth night."

"It's the shamash," Kamille said, leaning in, mouth full. "The helper candle. It lights all the others."

Ella looked back at her own menorah, unwrapped now under the lights, and counted the branches with one fingertip like a suspicious merchant. Nine. Eight for the nights of the holiday, and one extra, set apart, a little taller or a little forward of the rest. All those years she had looked at it and seen a symmetrical object, and it had never once been symmetrical. It had been nine, always nine, one of which existed only to give light away. She did the sum again, out loud, feeling slightly ridiculous and entirely certain: four candles for four nights, plus the shamash, five. She'd been short one candle every time she'd counted before, and it had never mattered, because her grandmother had always set up the menorah before Ella got to the table.

"We need one more," she said. "I brought four."

"Take one of mine," said Mr. Bighorn, holding out his box, and Ella had the small, melancholic realization that this was the first year the box had been hers to bring at all, and she had brought it wrong, and it had turned out fine anyway, which felt like a summary of something but she refused to say so out loud.

By full dark they had both menorahs lit on the community table, hers and the borrowed one, and Sameer had claimed the job of holding the shamash's match "for safety," which everyone understood meant for glory. The fourth-night flames stood in a neat ascending line, and behind them the stage broke into a song Kamille knew and Ella half knew, and Sameer was humming it wrong on purpose to annoy her.

"You're going to light your sleeve," Ella said.

"I'm going to light the whole street," said Sameer, and held the match higher.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The restaurant had pushed its tables together under the big screen, and by the fourth quarter Mackenzie's whole row of family and friends had stopped ordering food and started ordering only the free refills. Her uncle kept standing up and sitting down like a jack-in-the-box with a bad hinge. Next to Mackenzie, Kailyn had both fists pressed to her mouth, and when the kicker's attempt sailed through the uprights with two seconds left, Kailyn screamed so loudly that a waiter carrying a tray paused mid-step and let the applause undulate past him before moving on.

"We won," Kailyn said. She said it again, louder, to Mackenzie's father across the table. "We won, we actually won."

Mackenzie had known Kailyn since sophomore year and had never once seen her at a game, watched a quarter on television with her, or heard her say the university's name without yawning. Now Kailyn was wearing the spare team sweatshirt Mackenzie's mother had brought, sleeves too long, cuffs over her hands. Mackenzie herself had spent the evening explaining pass interference to her little cousin, and she had deliberately not worn any team gear, because she liked the team fine but did not like being the kind of person who dressed up like a costume of herself. She was chewing on this difference, between Kailyn's joy and her own restraint, when she remembered something.

In psych last semester, Ms. Lewandowski had put a study on the projector, one Mackenzie had skimmed for the quiz and then filed away. Robert Cialdini, 1976. She pulled out her phone under the table and searched until she found it again. Students wore more of their university's clothing after the football team won, and when they described a win they said "we," and when they described a loss, they didn't. She read it twice. It wasn't a criticism of Kailyn, exactly. It was more like a mirror.

"Check this out," she said, angling the screen toward Kailyn. "That thing you just did. There's a whole study about it."

Kailyn leaned in, still glowing, and her face did something complicated while she read. "So he's saying I'm, what, borrowing the win?"

"I think he's saying everybody does. It's not just you." Mackenzie hesitated, because she did not want to hand Kailyn a reason to feel stupid on the best night of her semester. Kailyn's applications were due in eleven days and her essay had been drafted and deleted four times; she had been saying for weeks that she needed one thing, any thing, to go right. This game had gone right. "It's kind of nice, actually. That people can share in something they didn't do."

Kailyn was quiet for a moment, thumbs moving in the too-long sleeves. "But you didn't put on the sweatshirt my mom offered you." That was true, and Mackenzie felt caught by it, the way the study sat in her phone between them like a small piece of evidence. She had thought of her restraint as probity, some small personal integrity about not claiming what wasn't hers, and now she wondered whether it was only a different flavor of the same thing, managing her reflection in the team's shine. Maybe refusing to say "we" was still talking about yourself. She hadn't settled that, and she said so.

"I don't know," Mackenzie said. "Maybe I'm doing it backwards. Being proud of not taking credit is still, like, a move."

Ms. Lewandowski was three tables over, grading papers beside a half-eaten plate of nachos, and on her way out she stopped at their row. "Congratulations," she said to the table generally, and then, to Mackenzie, with a small raised eyebrow: "I saw the phone. Chapter seven." Mackenzie laughed and admitted it, and Ms. Lewandowski said only, "It holds up," and left a twenty toward the bill before anyone could argue.

Kailyn had gone back to her own phone, and now she turned the screen around. The first line of her college essay, retyped, began: I have never played a down of football in my life, and last Saturday I wore a stranger's sweatshirt and screamed "we won." Her eyes were wet. "Is it terrible? Be honest, but gently." Around them the restaurant was emptying, and the big screen had switched to a talk show, and a busboy was stacking chairs with a patience that felt seismic in the quiet after all that noise.

Mackenzie pulled Kailyn's sleeve down off her hand, the way you do for a little kid, and started reading.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
Madison had signed up because her guidance counsellor said colleges liked to see volunteering, and because the alternative was a Saturday at home watching her mother alphabetize the spice rack. The soup kitchen occupied the basement of a church whose basement smelled like dish steam and floor wax, and by ten in the morning it was already loud. A man at the counter was arguing with a cashier about whether he could substitute juice for the tomatoes in his hamper, and the cashier, choleric in a way that suggested this was the third such argument of the morning, was holding firm.

"You're on hamper packing," said Ms. Santoso, the coordinator, without looking up from her clipboard. "Aprons are on the hook. Mohamed will show you the sheet."

Mohamed was already at the long table, checking items off a list against a cardboard box. He was in Madison's chemistry class, though they had never spoken, and he greeted her with the relieved politeness of someone who had been alone in a basement full of shouting. The system was simple, he explained: each family had a sheet, and the sheet said how many adults, how many children, what allergies. You built the box to match. He handed her a sheet and she began.

The third sheet she picked up said four children. The fourth said three. She found herself walking back to the shelf of baby formula and toddler snacks again and again, juice boxes and granola bars and jars of pureed fruit, and she started keeping a tally in the margin of one sheet out of something she couldn't quite name, because it wasn't assigned and nobody had asked. It was more like the feeling of a wrong answer in a textbook, an itch to check her work.

"Where's Angelica?" she asked, mostly to break the rhythm of the tally.

"Break. She's on the flyer run." Mohamed taped a box shut and reached past her for the formula. "She wants the volunteer coordinator credit for her application, so she's trying to redesign the whole intake system. She made Ms. Santoso a PowerPoint. On her own laptop. With transitions."

Angelica arrived at eleven with a stack of flyers and a grievance. Ms. Santoso had said the PowerPoint was interesting, which Angelica interpreted, correctly, as a rejection. There followed a detente of about forty minutes in which Angelica packed hampers with pointed efficiency and Ms. Santoso signed off on sheets at the far end of the table, until Angelica cracked first and went to ask about the break schedule, which was, everyone understood, merely a pretext.

At the sorting shelf, Madison counted her margin. Out of the twenty-six hampers they'd built that morning, the sheets listed children on what looked to her like more than eight, close to nine. She did the division on the inside of a cereal box. "Mohamed. Is it always like this? This many kids on the sheets?"

He glanced at her tally, then at the wall, where a poster she hadn't read yet was taped beside the fire exit. "You haven't seen the poster," he said. "Children were about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. It's from Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report. They put it up when they got the new numbers." He said it the way he said everything, flat and quick, and went back to taping.

A third. She looked down the table at the boxes, at the row of juice boxes standing in them like small bricks, and thought of the statistics unit in math, where a third had always meant a pie chart, nothing you could lift. She had come for a line on an application, and she was starting to suspect the line would be the least of what she carried out. At the same time she didn't want to be the person who performed her concern, the one who told the story at dinner in a voice that made it about her. Angelica's PowerPoint and her own tally sheet were maybe the same mistake from opposite directions, and Madison hadn't yet worked out what the third direction was, or whether there was one.

The morning rush thinned. Ms. Santoso came down the table collecting finished sheets, and paused at Madison's cereal box with its long column of marks. "You counted," she said, in the tone of someone noticing a plant that had come up without being watered. She didn't say anything else about it, just set a fresh stack of sheets on the table, and the stack was noticeably thicker than the last one.

Madison sharpened the pencil against the box edge and reached for the first sheet. Four adults, six children. She started down the aisle toward the formula shelf, and behind her she heard Angelica ask Ms. Santoso, "So about the break schedule," and Mohamed, not looking up, begin to laugh.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, both women's hearts are exposed, and a single blood vessel connects them, winding through their hands and hearts.
story:
The print of The Two Fridas was taped to the whiteboard at a slight angle, and Hailey kept noticing the angle when she meant to be noticing the painting. Mr. López had given them forty minutes and a single instruction: describe what you see before you decide what it means. Color, composition, symbolism, in that order, and no skipping ahead. Around her the art room smelled of turpentine and the glue somebody had spilled on Tuesday and never fully cleaned, and the radiators ticked with a glacial kind of heat, warm enough to argue with the January windows but not warm enough to win.

She had a page of notes already. The Frida on the left in a white European dress, the one on the right in a Tehuana dress, green skirt, blue blouse. Storm sky behind them, clouds the color of a bruise healing. Two benches, one nearly empty, holding a few shriveled hearts and veins that looked like string. She was less sure about the composition. The figures were symmetrical and still, like a portrait, but the sky behind them moved, and that contradiction seemed important in a way she couldn't yet write down.

"What if I can't get past what it means," she said to Izaiah, who sat beside her sketching the composition in pencil, fast little strokes. "I already know she painted it right after her divorce. That's all I can think about."

"That's your problem, not the painting's," Izaiah said, without looking up. "Look at the hands."

She looked. Each woman held something. The European Frida, on the left, held a small pair of scissors, and near her sleeve the paint showed a drop of red at the end of a vein, cut. The Tehuana Frida, on the right, held a small oval frame, a portrait of someone as a child. Between them their hands met in the middle of the canvas, almost touching, and something ran through those hands.

Hailey leaned closer to the print. "Wait," she said. "Both of them. Look at the chests."

Both women's hearts were exposed, painted whole and anatomical, red against white fabric and blue blouse. A single blood vessel connected them, winding through their hands and hearts, a pale red line looping from one chest down through the joined hands and up into the other chest. It was the only thing in the painting that physically joined the two figures. Everything else, the sky, the benches, the separate dresses, divided them.

Izaiah was tracing it already, his pencil traveling the route on his sketch, down from the left heart through the left hand, across, through the right hand, up to the right heart. "One vein," he said. "One vein for two people."

"Vessel," Hailey said, and then, quieter, "or vein, whatever. It's one, though. It's the same line." She had been ready to write a paragraph about isolation and heartbreak, the cut artery, the storm, all of it biographical, and now the painting was handing her something structural instead. The scissors cut the line on the left side, but the line itself went on. She wrote: the connection is literal, not symbolic. Then she crossed out "not symbolic" because that wasn't right either. The connection was literal and symbolic at once, and she didn't know how to say both in one sentence.

From where Laurence sat across the room, the whole discussion looked like a scene from a distance, two heads bent over a sketch, the print shining under the fluorescents. He had finished his own analysis early and mostly by pretending. His mother had eulogized Kahlo once at a dinner party, calling her an icon of suffering and survival, an aphorism for every occasion, and Laurence had absorbed the idea that the paintings were illustrations of a life story, captions without needing to look. Watching Hailey now, frowning at her crossed-out sentence, tapping her pen, he understood that he had never actually looked at one for more than four seconds.

He got up and crossed the room. "What did you find?"

"One vein," Hailey said. "Between them. Through the hands." Izaiah turned the sketch so Laurence could see the traced red route, and Laurence looked at the print for a long moment, actually looked, and said, "Huh. I always thought they were just holding hands."

"It's more than that," Hailey said. "It's like the painting says they're one person with two bodies, and then the scissors say, and also you can bleed out."

Mr. López drifted past their table, coffee cup in hand, and read over Hailey's shoulder without commenting. He underlined nothing, offered nothing, only said, "Ten minutes," and moved on. Hailey appreciated that about him. Last semester her English teacher had explained every poem before anyone could misread it, which meant no one ever got to misread it, and Hailey had learned less in that class than any other.

She remembered, then, being eleven and deciding she hated museums because a guide had told her what a painting was about, in a voice that closed the subject. She had chosen, without knowing she was choosing, to let other people do her looking for her. Maybe that was too harsh a verdict on her eleven-year-old self. She was still deciding whether it was.

In the last ten minutes she wrote her paragraph. Formal analysis first: complementary color, the warm red of the hearts against the cool blues and the white; bilateral symmetry holding two figures in an uneasy stillness; the exposed hearts, the single connecting vessel winding through hands and hearts, cut on one side and intact on the other. Then, and only then, symbolism, where she argued that the painting insisted on connection even while it depicted a severing, and admitted in her final sentence that she could not tell whether the vein was meant as a wound or a lifeline, and that the painting might refuse to choose. She read it over once. It wasn't finished, but it was honest.

When the bell rang, Izaiah tore his sketch along the margin, folded it, and set it beside her notebook, the traced red line still visible through the fold. "For your paragraph," he said, and shouldered his bag.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1, for every n except negative 1.
story:
Lauren had signed up for math club in September mostly because Aliza did, and because the physics room on Thursday afternoons was warm and empty and no one asked her anything. By November the club had shrunk to five people and a moribund attendance sheet that Mr. Balogun, the advisor, kept taping back onto the wall beside the periodic table. He never taught them anything. He sat at the front grading quizzes and occasionally said, "You're overcomplicating it," which was not helpful but was, Lauren had to admit, usually true.

That Thursday he had put a single problem on the board: find the area under the curve y equals x squared, from zero to two. "You haven't been taught integration," he said. "So invent it." Then he went back to his quizzes, and the five of them stared at the board the way people stare at a door they don't have a key to.

Lindsay started by drawing rectangles under the curve, thin ones, then thinner, counting. "If you use a hundred of them you get close," she said, "but it's an approximation forever. You never land." Aliza, meanwhile, had gone at it from the other direction, working out a rule: if you wanted the antiderivative of x to the power n, you wrote x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1. She tested it against x squared and x cubed and it kept working. Lauren copied her method into her notebook, ran the numbers, and got eight thirds, which the textbook in the back of the room confirmed. Eight thirds. Not approximately. Exactly.

Lauren had spent the previous summer helping her uncle paint houses, and there was a moment she kept coming back to now: standing on a ladder estimating how much paint a wall would take, knowing the wall's edges were straight and the answer would be honest. A curve was not a wall. A curve lied about its area, or seemed to, and she liked that someone had found a way to pin it down anyway, to codify the slanting, sliding shape into a single fraction. She was not, by her own account, a math person. She was a person who had once been good at math and then, somewhere in tenth grade, had decided she wasn't, in the same way she'd decided she didn't run anymore after quitting track. Both decisions had felt final at the time. Neither had ever really been examined.

So she stayed after the others left, and Aliza stayed with her, and they tried the rule on other functions to see where it broke. Lauren picked x to the negative one, which was one over x, because it was the simplest thing left on the list. She wrote out the rule carefully: x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1. Then she stopped. "It's negative one," she said. "n plus one is zero. I'm dividing by zero."

Aliza leaned over. "So the rule just dies there?"

"The rule doesn't die. It just doesn't apply. It works for every power except negative one." Lauren looked at the graph she'd sketched in the margin, one over x, its two arms sweeping away from the axes. There was a word for that kind of retreat, one she'd half remembered from a lesson she'd daydreamed through. "An asymptote," she said. "The graph never touches the axes. It gets close forever and never lands." Lindsay's rectangles, she thought. Same problem. Some things you approach and never arrive at, and maybe the rule breaking at negative one was that same idea wearing different clothes, though she couldn't have said exactly how, and she wasn't going to pretend she could.

She thought of quitting track again, briefly, the way she thought of it most weeks. She had told everyone she'd been too slow. The truth was she'd been fast enough to make the relay team and had walked away the week before the meet because she was afraid of being the one who dropped the baton, and no one had asked her a second time. Here, nobody was asking her to be a math person either. Mr. Balogun had said invent it, and she and Aliza had invented most of a rule and then found its exact edge, the one place where the whole tidy machine refused to run, and that felt like more than she'd managed in a long time.

She wrote the exception in the margin of her notes and boxed it, twice, the way she boxed things she didn't trust herself to remember. "Next week," she said to Aliza, "I want to know what you're supposed to do about one over x. There has to be something."

"There doesn't have to be," Aliza said, pulling on her coat.

Lauren looked at the asymptote in her margin, its arms forever approaching and never arriving, and left it on the page, unboxed, open.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key, so a movement in C major moves to G major.
story:
The music room smelled of valve oil and old radiator dust, and Jackson had the photocopied score of Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, flattened on the upright piano's music desk like something he intended to interrogate. He did intend to interrogate it. The exam was in nine days, and Ms. Lau had told them, more than once, that she could tell the difference between a student who had heard the form and a student who had memorized a diagram. Jackson had memorized the diagram. Exposition, development, recapitulation, three boxes with arrows between them, and he could not for the life of him hear where one ended and the next began.

Lane arrived eight minutes late with two coffees and handed one over without apology, which was how Lane did most things. She sat on the piano bench beside him, closer than strictly necessary, and pulled the score toward her side of the desk. "Play it," she said. "You're the one who needs it in your ears. I already passed this exam."

"You failed it last year."

"I deferred it. There's a difference." She nudged his elbow off the keys. "Play."

He played the opening, the part every child in every piano studio in every city had played, the melody so familiar it had desensitized him to it, the way a word repeated forty times stops meaning anything. Somewhere around measure twenty a second tune arrived, singing and smoothing, and Jackson stopped with his hands still on the keys. "There. That's the second theme. I think."

"So mark it."

He picked up the pencil, held it over the bar line, and did not make the mark. Because Madisyn, who was sprawled in the chair by the window with her annotated score, the one Ms. Lau had praised in front of the whole class, the one with colour-coded brackets, had said something in the hallway two weeks ago that he had not been able to shake. She'd said that marking the form was a kind of violence, that Mozart had not written brackets, and that people who reduced a sonata to three labelled boxes were the opposite of aesthetes, they were accountants. She had said it lightly, tossing her bag over her shoulder, but he had felt it land somewhere under his ribs and lodge there. He had spent two years telling anyone who would listen that he wanted to be a musician, not a theorist. That theory was for people who couldn't feel anything.

"I don't know where it actually starts," he said to Lane, which was half true. "The tune kind of eases in."

"That's the whole trick of it, isn't it." Lane pulled the score back and squinted at the key signature. "Look at the accidentals after this line. There's a sharp showing up everywhere. F sharp, over and over."

Jackson looked. He had noticed the sharp earlier and filed it away as decoration, one of those things Mozart sprinkled through a melody the way his grandmother put paprika in everything. But now he counted them, followed the line of harmony down the page, and felt something rearrange itself in his understanding. The second theme wasn't just a new tune. It had moved. The movement was in C major, and this new melody, this second theme in the exposition, was sitting in G major, the dominant. He said it out loud to hear whether it sounded true. "It's gone to G. C to G." The second theme of the exposition, in the dominant key. He drew the bracket, and this time the pencil did not hesitate.

"Congratulations," Lane said. "You've discovered the eighteenth century."

He played the passage again, and the modulation was suddenly audible, a door he had walked past a hundred times without knowing it was a door. It was not that Madisyn was wrong, exactly. He understood what she meant about the brackets. But sitting here with the sharp signs marching down the page, he found he could not accept that hearing the structure took anything away from the sound, that knowing where the door was made the room smaller. It felt, if anything, like the opposite: the tune he had been deaf to was suddenly part of an argument, a departure and a promise of return. He thought of his father, who had wanted him to study something practical, and of Madisyn, who had made theory sound like a betrayal, and he noticed that both of them wanted him to feel a certain way about the same eight bars of Mozart, and neither of them was here.

The door opened and Ms. Lau came in carrying a stack of folders, stopped, and looked at the score between them, at the fresh bracket in Jackson's handwriting. She raised her eyebrows. "Second theme?"

"G major," Jackson said. "It moves from C to G. The dominant."

She set the folders down and said nothing for a moment, which from her was as good as applause. "Play the development for me when you get there. Tell me where Mozart starts hiding things."

He nodded and turned the page, and Lane slid off the bench to give him room, and outside the window the January light was going grey over the parking lot. His pencil was warm in his hand from holding it too long. He put it down on the ledge of the piano, flexed his fingers, and began to play.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
story:
Grandfather's house smelled of dust and pipe smoke that had outlived the pipe, and Laurie had been sent there for the weekend with a report to finish and instructions not to disturb the books. Ms. Fitzgerald had assigned each student a figure from the medieval world, and Laurie had drawn Marco Polo, which everyone agreed was the good pick. Faisal, on the phone from the city, had groaned about getting some abbot nobody had heard of, and Abygaelle had already written two pages about a queen and called it done. Laurie had less than nothing: a title page with her name spelled correctly and one sentence about a journey to China.

The report was due Monday, which was the problem. The solution, she decided, was the tall shelf in the back room, the one her grandfather called his library and everyone else called the overflow. She was not disturbing the books so much as consulting them, a distinction she was prepared to defend.

The shelf gave up a surprising amount. There was a fat orange paperback with a cracked spine, a modern popular history full of italics, which said Marco Polo had gone to China and stayed seventeen years in the service of Kublai Khan, which was the version Laurie had always known, the version in the textbook, the version with the illustrations of camels. Fine. She copied a quote about the wealth of the East and felt the report begin to exist.

Then she found the other book. It was slimmer, the jacket gone gray along the edges, and it was by a historian named Frances Wood, and its argument stopped her with her hand still on the shelf. Frances Wood had argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China at all. She pointed out that his book never mentions tea, never mentions foot-binding, never mentions the Great Wall. Laurie read the list twice, then went to the window and looked out at the garden, where her grandfather's roses were going over early this year, a small annual entropy she was used to and usually ignored.

She texted Abygaelle, who texted back a shrug in emoji form and then, when pressed, an actual sentence: which book do you trust? Laurie demurred. Trusting books had never seemed like something you had to choose about before. The orange paperback said China plainly, in italics, as though italics were evidence. The gray book said "may never have reached," which was weaker and somehow harder to dismiss, because the person writing it had clearly thought about tea.

At supper she put it to her grandfather, who was eating bread and honey with the concentration of a man who had been asked no questions all week. "I'm doing Marco Polo," she said. "One book says he went to China. Another says maybe he never got there. His book never even mentions the Great Wall."

Her grandfather chewed for a while. "Your grandmother had two cookbooks," he said finally. "One said you brown the onions first. The other said you never brown the onions. I ate forty years of onions." He went back to his honey, and Laurie sat there feeling that something had been said, though she could not have repeated it for a grade.

She called Faisal instead. Faisal, who was doing an abbot, was instantly, insultingly delighted. "Wait, so the most famous traveler in history might not have gone anywhere?"

"That's not the point."

"Then what's the point?"

"The point is nobody was there to check. There's just his book, and the book doesn't mention tea, and a billion people drink tea, so either he wasn't paying attention or he wasn't there, and I have to write one page about this by Monday and I don't know which page is true." She heard her own voice climb and brought it down.

"Write both," Faisal said, in the tone of someone handing over a problem rather than solving it.

Sunday afternoon she sat on the floor of the back room with both books open in front of her, an arrangement that struck her as faintly atavistic, two rival paper tribes facing each other across her knees. She wrote the paragraph from the orange book. Then she wrote: however, the historian Frances Wood has argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall. She looked at the two sentences, the italics on one side and the hedge on the other, and wrote beneath them a third: which account you believe may depend on which question you were asking. She did not know if that was a conclusion. She suspected it was more like a door with weather on both sides of it.

Monday, after the reports, Ms. Fitzgerald kept her a moment. "The Wood book," she said. "Where did you find that?"

"My grandfather's house."

"Tell him thank you." Ms. Fitzgerald was stacking the pages, not looking up. "And Laurie. The paragraph ends on a question. That's allowed, you know. Sometimes it's the honest place to stop."

Laurie walked out past the trophy case, where the class photo from 1974 showed thirty faces all certain about something, and thought about telephoning her grandfather to relay the thank you, and decided instead to write it in a letter, a thing she had never done, and which seemed, suddenly, like the right size for what she wanted to say. She bought a stamp at the corner store and licked the envelope in the doorway.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
The diagram on Daniel's lab bench had eleven arrows, and he was almost certain all of them were wrong. He had drawn them at the start of the period, quick and confident, pointing from the negative plate toward the positive plate, because it had seemed obvious that the negative plate would pull and the positive plate would just sit there. Now, twenty minutes later, he kept turning the paper sideways as if a new angle might make the thing resolve.

"You're hovering," Tiffany said from the next stool. She was calibrating their voltmeter, or pretending to; mostly she was watching him rotate the sheet like a steering wheel. "Just pick a direction."

"That's the problem. I picked one." He slid the paper toward her. "Emmitt says the arrows go the other way."

Tiffany set down the probe. Across the lab, Emmitt was doing something theatrical with a ruler, holding it between two hands like a tiny balance beam, and Ms. Haddad was circulating between benches with her arms folded behind her, the way she did when she wanted them to forget she was there.

"Come look," Daniel called to him, and Emmitt arrived trailing the smell of the hand sanitizer by the sink.

"Okay, so," Emmitt said, tapping the negative plate on the diagram. "Think about it like a test charge. If you put a proton in there, between the plates. Which way would it move?"

"Toward the negative plate," Tiffany said. "Opposites attract. Everybody knows that."

"Right. A positive charge gets pushed away from the positive plate and toward the negative plate." Emmitt drew a single arrow in the margin, left to right, positive to negative. "So the electric field points that way. From positive toward negative."

Daniel looked at the margin arrow, then at his eleven backwards arrows, and felt the specific sting of having been confident in the wrong direction. He had argued with Emmitt about it for half of lunch, and Emmitt had not argued back so much as wait, which was worse.

"Then why did I draw them like this?"

"Because it feels like the negative plate is doing the pulling," Emmitt said. "I did the same thing last night. I had to do the problem three times before I believed it."

That was the part Daniel had not expected. He had assumed Emmitt was the kind of person who just knew things, who read the chapter once and it stuck, while Daniel had to build every idea out of scrap. Hearing that Emmitt had also gotten it backwards did not aggrandize either of them, exactly; it just made the mistake a shared country instead of a private one.

"So wait," Tiffany said. "The field isn't about what the negative plate wants. It's about what would happen to a positive charge in between. The direction a proton would get pushed."

"From positive toward negative," Daniel said, and Emmitt nodded.

Ms. Haddad drifted over, looked at the diagram without touching it, and said only, "You've marked the positive plate on the left?" When Daniel said yes, she raised an eyebrow at his arrows, said "Interesting," and moved on, which was her way of letting a person keep their dignity and their error at the same time.

Daniel erased all eleven arrows. The rubber left a gray smear across the middle of the page, and he redrew them carefully, each one starting at the positive plate and ending short of the negative one, because the field filled the space between but did not need to be dramatic about it. He thought of it as an auxiliary rule, a smaller thing you kept beside the main one: when in doubt, ask where the proton goes. The proton was honest. It did not care which plate he found more intuitive.

Then he did the calculation, field strength at the midpoint, and checked it against Tiffany's meter reading, and the numbers agreed to within the tolerance she'd written at the top of her page in purple ink. He had wanted the lab to feel like a curve approaching its asymptote, getting closer and closer to some perfect understanding, but this was more like a door. One minute the arrows were backwards, and the next they were not, and he could not quite reconstruct the before.

He copied the corrected diagram onto a second sheet and handed it to Emmitt. "For your notes. Since yours has the margin version only."

Emmitt took it. "You drew it neater than mine."

"I had more arrows to fix."

Tiffany laughed, and Daniel, gathering the probes into their case, noticed her voltmeter was still on, its battery draining quietly into the bench, and reached over and switched it off for her. She said thanks without looking up. At the front of the room, Ms. Haddad began pulling the blinds, and the last of the afternoon light lay flat across the two plates of Daniel's diagram, positive on the left, all the arrows pointing home.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
The invitation had arrived in December, folded into Michael's backpack by his grandmother's own hand, and it specified January 7, which was why he had spent three weeks believing it was a typo. His grandmother did not make typos. She made borscht, and threats about his posture, and appointments. When he'd asked his mother why they were doing Christmas two weeks after the neighbors had dragged their trees to the curb, she said, "Because we just do," in the voice she used for weather and for his grandfather.

He got the real answer from Aydin, of all people, over cafeteria fries that last day before break. Aydin's family went to a Russian Orthodox church downtown, and when Michael complained about the January 7 thing, Aydin laughed so hard he inhaled a fry. "That's my Christmas too," Aydin said. "Many Orthodox churches keep it then. They hold December 25 on the old Julian calendar, so it lands on January 7 for us." Michael said, "That's insane," and Aydin said, "That's heritage," and they'd both laughed, but on the bus home Michael kept turning it over. Two Christmases existed on the same street, and his whole life he'd thought the second one was just his family being difficult.

The difficulty arrived on January 6 in the form of Annabelle's text: her birthday party, the one she'd been planning since November, was tomorrow at two, and she had put him on the list for the escape room, and the escape room needed exactly six people or the booking collapsed. Michael stood in his grandmother's kitchen, holding his phone in one hand and a bag of walnuts in the other, and felt the two halves of his life slide toward each other like tectonic plates. Dinner at grandmother's was at three. The escape room was at two. Both were tomorrow, both were immovable, and both, he suspected, were partly a test of which Michael would show up.

"You look like a walnut yourself," his grandmother said, taking the bag from him. "Sit. Shell."

He sat at the counter with the nutcracker and decided that if he was going to disappoint somebody, he would at least understand what he was disappointing them for. "Baba, why January 7? Like, actually why?"

She cracked a walnut with a violence that suggested the walnut owed her money. "Because your grandfather's people were Russian Orthodox, and the church keeps the old calendar, and so we keep Christmas when the church keeps it. Also because I say so." That last part was delivered with such finality that Michael understood it was the load-bearing wall of the whole operation. Behind it, though, was something else: the calendar was the reason, but the dinner was the point. His grandfather had died in the spring, and this was the first Christmas dinner without him, and his grandmother had invited eleven relatives, some of whom had not spoken to each other since a funeral-related dispute over a car.

"Who's coming tomorrow?" he asked, as if idly.

"Everyone," she said, in the tone of a general announcing that the entire biome of her apartment would be occupied by family by three o'clock, that the living room would be rendered impervious to escape by uncles and folding chairs. Michael looked at the nut pile, at the mountain of food already staged in the refrigerator, at the photograph of his grandfather by the stove, and did the arithmetic he had been avoiding. Annabelle had five other friends who could conceivably be drafted. His grandmother had no alternative grandson who knew where the good dishes were stored and which uncle had to be seated away from which aunt.

He texted Aydin first, because Aydin would understand. "You doing anything tomorrow besides Christmas?" Aydin replied with a photograph of his own family's kitchen, equally catastrophic, and the words "help me." So Michael called Annabelle, and told her the truth, which was that his family celebrated Christmas on January 7 because the old Julian calendar put December 25 there, and that this year the dinner was not optional. He waited for her to be furious. Instead there was a pause, and then she said, "That's actually the best excuse I've ever heard. My grandma still writes me letters in cursive, I get it. But you owe me, and the debt compounds."

The next afternoon he carried dishes, deflected an uncle's opinions about his future, and found himself seated between two relatives who had not spoken in a year, a position he had not chosen but which he slowly realized he could use. He asked each of them, separately, for the story of the car. The stories contradicted each other in every detail except the ending, and by dessert they were arguing about it directly, which was not reconciliation but was, his grandmother whispered to him, at least conversation. She squeezed his wrist. "Your grandfather would have started that fight on purpose," she said. "You started it by accident. Better technique."

Late that night, back home, he texted Annabelle a photo of the wreckage of the table, and she texted back a photo of the escape room team holding a sign that said WE FAILED WITHOUT MICHAEL. He laughed, then sat with the phone dark in his hand, thinking that he still wasn't sure he'd chosen right, only that he'd chosen for a reason he could actually name. Tomorrow he would start paying down the debt. He typed, "Compounding rate?" and waited, smiling, for her answer.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The party had spilled from Miya's kitchen onto the back steps, where the August air smelled of citronella and somebody's older brother's cigarettes. Jake stood near the door with a paper cup of flat ginger ale, listening to Maelle describe the apartment his family was renting, which she had apparently looked up online, a spartan two-bedroom above a hardware store in a town none of them could picture. "You'll be back at Thanksgiving," she said, "and it'll be like you never left."

He wanted that to be true, and he also wanted the opposite, and he could not make himself say which. So he said, "There's a lake, apparently. The realtor kept saying lake." Miya interposed herself between them with a bowl of chips and said the realtor had probably said that to everyone, and they laughed, and the conversation moved on to the drive-through run Maelle was proposing at eleven.

Jake had spent the summer reading, which was unlike him. It started when he was trying to find out whether it was possible to keep friends at a distance, whether the thing people said about long friendships dying was a law or a habit. Somewhere in that search he had landed on a paper by a sociologist named Mark Granovetter, published in 1973, called "The Strength of Weak Ties." The finding was simple and strange: people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. He had read it twice, then closed the laptop and felt vaguely insulted, as if the paper had told him his friendships were structurally useless.

"You're doing the face," Miya said, appearing beside him on the steps. The others had gone inside; her breath fogged though it was not cold. "The moving-away face. Where you go somewhere we can't follow and feel bad about it alone."

"I read something," he said. "Granovetter, 1973. The Strength of Weak Ties." He told her the finding, holding the cup with both hands. "So the people you barely know are worth more than the people you'd die for. Professionally speaking."

"That's the saddest sentence anyone has ever said to me at a party," Miya said. But she was quiet for a moment after, tapping the rail. "Maelle got her job at the clinic because her mom's friend mentioned it. She's met the woman twice in her life."

Jake considered this. He had assumed Maelle's job had come through the school, through the ordinary machinery of guidance counselors and posted flyers. It had come through a neighbor she could not, at that moment, probably have named.

Ms. De Vries arrived late, carrying a lemon cake in a box tied with kitchen twine, because she had taught all three of them in tenth grade and still lived four houses down and believed in cake at departures. She asked Jake practical questions, and he answered them in the practical voice he used with adults, and then she asked whether he would have a job there, in the new town.

"Probably not," he said. "I'll be the new kid. New kids don't have contacts."

"Everyone has contacts," she said. "My sister runs the café on Mulberry, the one with the blue awnings. I'll tell her a decent young man is arriving, if you like." She said it lightly, the way people offer things they expect to be declined. She had met Jake exactly twice in three years, once at a bake sale and once when his father's car blocked her driveway.

He said yes, and gave her his number, and watched her write it in the margin of a crossword puzzle folded in her purse. Inside, Maelle and Miya were arguing about the drive-through with the intensity of people avoiding a different subject, and the citronella candle on the rail had guttered into a pool of wax with a blackened wick standing in it. It was possible, he thought, that his real friends were the ones who knew him, and it was also possible that the whole year ahead would be built out of people like Ms. De Vries, brief and useful and kind in passing, and he could not decide which of those mattered more, or whether the question was even fair to either side. He did not have to decide tonight. He went inside to find his jacket, and Miya held it out to him already, without a word.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
story:
Audrey had reserved the study room at the public library for two hours, and she was determined not to waste the second one the way she had wasted the first, which was to say reading the same paragraph of her textbook four times while her phone sat face down and buzzing like a trapped insect. The assignment was to weigh two historians' explanations of the Cold War against the evidence, and so far the evidence was winning, in the sense that it had defeated her completely.

Myah arrived twelve minutes late carrying a canvas bag that clinked. "Don't ask," she said, setting it on the table. Inside were four energy drinks, a highlighter in a color Audrey had never seen before, and a paperback with a cracked spine. "Myah, why do you have that."

"Grandpa's. I took it by accident when we visited, along with, like, three John Grishams." She slid it across. "He kept saying you'd want it. Something about your homework. He was weirdly excited. He wrote in it, so don't judge the margins."

The book was The Tragedy of American Diplomacy, and the copyright page said 1959. Audrey flipped it open and found a margin note in ballpoint, emphatically underlined, next to a passage about American economic expansion: "We did this to ourselves. Look it up." She looked at Myah, who shrugged and cracked an energy drink.

"Wait," Audrey said. "This guy. Williams. He's saying the United States helped cause the Cold War? Not just the Soviets?"

"That's what Grandpa said. He called it revisionist. He was very smug about it."

Audrey's textbook, open at page 640, subsumed the whole conflict under a heading called "Soviet Aggression and the American Response," which until an hour ago had seemed like a reasonable heading. Now it seemed like a choice someone had made. She pulled the book back toward her and read the paragraph again, this time noticing what it left out, which was a different thing from what it got wrong. The chapter described the Marshall Plan, the Truman Doctrine, the need for open markets, all in the tone of a nature documentary describing weather. Nobody in the chapter wanted anything. Everyone simply responded.

"Okay," she said slowly, "so the traditional view is that the Soviets started it and America defended itself. And this guy Williams says American economic expansion helped cause it. And my assignment is to decide which one the evidence supports, which would be fine if the evidence weren't the whole problem."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning the same fact fits both stories. The Marshall Plan either proves America was generous or proves America needed markets. The textbook never asks the second question. But Williams never really answers the first one either." She turned to a page in the paperback where the argument got dense and the ballpoint got denser. "Grandpa highlighted a lot."

Myah, who had been quietly building a tower out of her empty cans, had her own agenda, and now she deployed it. "So while you figure out the Cold War, I need you to look at my college essay. It's due Friday and it's bad. Mr. Park said I could email him the draft but I can't email a librarian, that's like admitting defeat."

"Mr. Park is here right now," Audrey said, because she could see him through the glass, reshelving at the far end of the stacks with the patience of a glacier.

"That's exactly the problem."

They compromised: Myah would print the essay from the library computers while Audrey worked, and then they would trade, Cold War for college essay, which struck Audrey as an exchange roughly as unequal as Lend-Lease. She kept reading. Williams wrote well, better than her textbook, but she caught herself doing the thing Mr. Park had warned her about at the reference desk last week, back when she'd asked him how to know if a source was biased: "Everyone's biased," he'd said, handing her a stack without ceremony. "The question is whether they show their work."

Williams showed his work. But she found a spot where he treated American intentions as settled, assumed rather than argued, and she wrote in the margin of her notebook, "How does he know they wanted markets more than security?" Then she wrote, under it, "How does the textbook know the opposite?" Neither question had a clean answer. That was the part nobody had warned her about, that evidence didn't arrive holding a sign explaining itself. The pragmatics of it were brutal: the same document could be exhibit A for either side depending on what you already believed came first.

Myah returned with the essay, four paragraphs about how a summer of detasseling corn had taught her resilience. Audrey read it and said, honestly, "The part about the truck driver is the good part. Everything else sounds like a fortune cookie."

"The truck driver's real, though."

"Then write about him more. Say less about lessons." Audrey slid the Cold War books into her bag. "I'm going to say both historians are partly tenable and the evidence underdetermines the answer. That's not a cop-out if I show which evidence leans which way. Right?" She stood. "I need to ask Mr. Park if we have Foreign Relations volumes. And also not to tell him about the essay, because that's your job."

Myah groaned. Audrey was already crossing the room, the paperback under her arm, Grandpa's underlines showing at the edges like a hand raised in the back of a classroom.

"Mr. Park," she said, "do you have the documents the State Department published themselves?"

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
Jade had parked in the last row of the lot, where the asphalt gave way to a chain-link fence and, beyond it, the creek the AP Environmental class had spent a semester calling the riparian corridor, though by June the sumac had grown high enough that you could mostly forget the water was there. Her gown was folded on the passenger seat, still creased from the bag. She was sixteen, a year early, and the fact had begun to feel less like an accomplishment and more like a door she had walked through before checking what was on the other side.

She had a want, and it was simple: she wanted her grandmother to come to the ceremony. Her grandmother had said maybe, which in her vocabulary meant no, and Jade had spent two weeks trying to convert a maybe into a yes without asking directly, the way you jiggle a stuck zipper rather than yank it.

Scarlett found her at the car, holding two Programs of Ceremony rolled like batons. "They want the early grads to stand when Ms. Liu calls your names," she said. "All eleven of you. Then everybody claps and feels amazed at you."

"I don't want to stand."

"Then sit. Nobody's going to drag you up." Scarlett's own want was larger and less private: she had been chosen to read the class poem, and she had rewritten it four times since Sunday, and she wanted, before three hundred folding chairs filled up, for one person to hear it aloud and tell her it didn't sound like a greeting card. "Come sit on the wall. I need ears."

They sat on the low concrete wall by the flagpole, and Scarlett read the poem, her voice flattening itself into bravado at the places she didn't trust. Jade listened. It was better than Scarlett thought and worse than Scarlett feared, which was the usual condition of things. "Keep the part about the parking lot," Jade said. "Cut the part about destiny."

From Scarlett's side of the wall, the lot looked different than it had all year: the spaces were emptying as families arrived, folding chairs rising out of the gym on hand trucks, Ms. Liu out front with a clipboard, taping a paper sign to the fence that read GRADUATES ASSEMBLE HERE. Scarlett watched Jade fold and unfold the corner of her gown's plastic sleeve and understood that something else was going on, that Jade's stillness wasn't calm but a held breath. "It's about your grandma," Scarlett said. Not a question.

"She never finished high school," Jade said. "I found her file in the shoebox when I was looking for stamps. A certificate. She took the GED tests. She told me once, after the army, but she never said when they started those. I looked it up at the library." Jade turned the plastic sleeve over. "They were created in 1942. So military service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school could show high-school-level skills."

"So she's got the same thing you're getting."

"She's got a different thing. She was in Trieste when she was my age. I was in biology maintaining homeostasis in a potato." It was the joke from the fall semester, the osmosis lab, and it landed the way old jokes land, in the chest rather than the ears.

Scarlett said, "Ask her what she thinks standing would mean. Not to you. To her." Then she stood, because Ms. Liu was waving the clipboard, and the graduates were supposed to line up, and the poem was still in her hand with destiny crossed out in pencil.

Jade's grandmother arrived at four, before the lot filled, driving the old car too slowly past the cones. She parked in the last row, beside Jade's, and sat for a moment with her hands on the wheel. Jade walked over in her gown, cap carried flat like a tray. Her grandmother looked at the gown a long time.

"You're standing with the early ones," her grandmother said. It was not a question either.

"If you sit in the third row I can see you from the stage."

"You can see me from anywhere, I'm not hiding." But she got out, and she smoothed her jacket, and she walked the line of cones as though reviewing them.

The ceremony itself was long. The principal's speech enraptured exactly the people who were already enraptured, parents with video cameras raised like votive candles. When Ms. Liu called the eleven names, Jade stood, and found she was scanning the third row without deciding to, and there her grandmother was, sitting very straight, her hands folded the way they must have been folded in waiting rooms and muster lines for seventy years.

Afterward, in the emptying lot, Scarlett found Jade by the fence above the creek. "Was it the poem or the standing that mattered more?" Scarlett asked, and Jade considered the question honestly, holding both answers, unwilling to discard either. "Ask me in ten years," she said. Behind the sumac, the water went on doing whatever it did, and the last folding chairs were stacked on the hand trucks, and her grandmother was still sitting in the third row, waiting for somebody to come tell her it was time to go.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Risk compensation is the tendency of people to behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted.
story:
Ms. Kaminski had written two words on the board before the bell finished ringing: intended outcomes, actual outcomes. Vanessa slid into her seat beside Elliott, who was already flipping through his notes on consequentialism, the view she had argued against for two weeks and was no longer sure she argued against at all. The assignment was to bring in one real decision from their own lives and trace what it had actually produced, not what they had meant to produce. Most people, Vanessa suspected, would invent something. She had something real, and she had spent the whole weekend not wanting to look at it.

In September, she had organized the petition to make helmets mandatory for the mountain biking club. It had seemed obvious, a small act of responsibility toward kids who raced down Corbett Hill with nothing between their skulls and the asphalt but confidence. The principal had approved it within a day, as though the school had been waiting for someone to reify the worry into a rule, to turn a vague fear into a policy with a signature at the bottom. Vanessa had felt proud of that signature. She still did, sometimes, and then she thought about Knox.

Knox showed up the first practice after the rule took effect with a new helmet, matte black, the kind with the sticker that promised a great deal. He had always been a careful rider, the one who braked for the hairpin where the fence had rusted through.
