That afternoon he took the hill faster than Vanessa had ever seen him go, standing on the pedals, taking the hairpin without touching the brakes, and when he reached the bottom he pulled up grinning and said the helmet made him feel invincible. She had laughed then. She did not laugh in October, when he clipped the fence at the same corner and needed eight stitches above his eyebrow, his helmet unmarked, his collarbone fractured in two places.

Ms. Kaminski asked who wanted to go first. Elliott raised his hand and talked about a group project he had taken over entirely, how his trade-off had been the others' grades against his own sleep, and how the outcome he had not predicted was that they had learned nothing and he had learned to resent them. Good, Ms. Kaminski said, that is an unintended consequence, and she wrote the phrase on the board beneath the others. Vanessa watched the chalk and felt the pieces begin to arrange themselves.

She raised her hand before she could decide against it. She told the helmet story plainly, the petition, the rule, Knox's black helmet, the speed, the collarbone. "I looked it up after Knox's crash," she said. "It's called risk compensation. People behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted." She kept her voice level, though Knox was sitting three rows back, his arm still in a sling. She did not turn around. "The rule I fought for didn't fail. Nobody hit their head. But I can't tell whether it helped or whether it just changed where the harm went."

Ms. Kaminski did not rescue her, which Vanessa both appreciated and resented. "So what does the consequentialist conclude?" she asked instead. Vanessa said she used to think consequentialism was cold, a way of reducing people to arithmetic. Now it seemed almost munificent compared with what she had done, because it at least demanded that she count everything, not just the harms she had set out to prevent. "But there's a version of responsibility that just follows the rules," she said, "and a version that looks at what the rules actually did, and I don't know how to live in the second one without becoming paralyzed." She heard her own voice waver on the last word and stopped.

After class, Knox was waiting by the door, sling and all. She braced for anger, or worse, for the generous forgiveness that would make her feel smaller. He did neither. "I signed your petition," he said. "Before the crash. I wanted the rule." He shifted his weight off the bad shoulder. "It's weird, right, that we both wanted the same thing and it still went wrong." Vanessa said yes, it was, and then asked if he wanted to walk out together, and he said he was going to the bike racks, he still rode, the helmet still worked, that was the whole problem. She laughed, and followed him down the corridor, and at the racks he swung his good leg over the frame and looked back at her. "Race you to the corner," he said. "Slowly."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The television in Grandpa's front room was older than Raphael, and it made the pitch look faintly green at the edges, as if the grass were unsure of itself. His grandfather had arranged the chairs in a crescent before kickoff, the way he did every final, and by the second half the room smelled of fried onions and cough sweets. Raphael sat on the floor between Denis and Kelly-Ann with his knees drawn up, while Denis leaned forward like a man being slowly pulled out of a window.

"Look at that number nine," Denis said, gesturing at the striker loitering behind the last defender. "He's been camping there all half. That's offside, that is. Every time."

"He's not doing anything," Kelly-Ann said. "He's just standing there."

"Standing there offside."

The clock in the corner read seventy-one minutes gone, and the match was still nil-nil, and Grandpa had begun his running commentary, half to the room and half to a cousin on the phone, lambasting the referee for every decision the man had made since the opening whistle, and a few he hadn't made at all. The score could change on one mistake now. That was the whole arithmetic of a final, and everyone in the crescent of chairs was doing it in their heads.

Then the corner came. The winger bent it in low and hard, and the number nine, the one Denis had been condemning for thirty minutes, rose at the near post and turned it into the net with a flick of his heel. The room erupted. Grandpa was on his feet, pointing at the screen with a remote control as though it were evidence. "Offside!" he bellowed. "He was offside all afternoon! Anyone with eyes saw it! The linesman's a disgrace!"

Denis stood up beside him, which surprised Raphael, because Denis had spent the season complaining about this exact player. "He's right," Denis said. "He was miles behind the defence. That has to be offside, surely."

Raphael felt something turn over in his chest, the strange vertigo of knowing a thing while everyone around you is certain of its opposite. He had played since he was seven, and somewhere along the line a coach had drilled it into him, one of those facts that sits in you like a stone. He got to his knees.

"It's not," he said. His voice came out smaller than he wanted, so he said it again. "There's no offside from a corner kick. It doesn't matter where he's standing. Throw-ins, goal kicks, corners, none of them count. You can't be offside from one."

Silence, except for the television, where the players were already jogging back for the restart and the replays were showing the kick from four angles, none of them finding anything.

"And anyway," Raphael went on, faster now, "he wasn't doing anything wrong just standing there. It's not an offence by itself. You only get penalized when you get involved, when you go for the ball or interfere. Before that it's nothing." He heard his own words pile up and worried they sounded like a lecture, but he couldn't stop them, because the match was still running and the clock was bleeding toward eighty minutes and if the goal stood or didn't, someone here would be wrong in front of everyone.

"Involved in active play," Kelly-Ann said slowly, her thumb already moving on her phone. "Hold on. Hold on, I'm checking." The room watched her instead of the screen. Grandpa lowered the remote control by degrees, like a flag coming down.

The phone glowed. "He's right," Kelly-Ann said. "It's right here. No offside from a corner. And being in the position isn't the offence on its own, he has to be involved in the play first."

Grandpa sat back down without a word. The cousin on the phone asked what had happened, and Grandpa said, "Nothing. A goal," in the flat voice of a raconteur who has just lost his best material. Denis remained standing a moment longer, insouciant for the length of a breath, then shrugged and dropped into his chair.

"You could have said something an hour ago," he told Raphael. "I've been calling him offside all match."

"You were half right," Raphael said. "He was in the position. He just wasn't doing anything about it. Not until the ball came."

"Same as me, then," Denis said. "Standing around, not involved." He grinned, and Grandpa made a noise that might have been a laugh.

On the screen, the other team pushed forward, desperate now, and in the eighty-ninth minute their striker was played through by a throw-in and buried his shot, and the whole room shouted at once, some standing, some pointing, Grandpa appealing to the ceiling. Raphael looked at the linesman's flag, still at his side, and felt the rules move under his feet like a floor he'd thought was solid.

The scoreboard in the corner began arranging itself for extra time. Kelly-Ann leaned over and said, "So explain the goal kick one again," and Raphael opened his mouth.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Computing a binary search's midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow on very large arrays; writing low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same middle without the overflow.
story:
Brooke's grandfather had cleared the dining table of his seed catalogs and let her spread the laptop, the notebook, and the printout of the practice problem across it, though every so often he drifted past with a querulous murmur about people who worked at tables where meals were meant to happen. Through the window behind him the garden was going brown at the edges, the last of the season, and the light came in low and yellow, which meant she had about two hours before the glare made the screen unreadable.

Zaid arrived at four with his bike helmet still on and a folder of contest datasets under his arm. Kayson came behind him, carrying the box of clementines Brooke's grandmother always set out for visitors whether or not they wanted any. The regional competition was in nine days, and their coach had excoriated the whole team at the last practice for submitting code that passed the samples and then fell over on the real data, so today they were going to run everything, every dataset, before touching anything new.

Brooke's part was the search. She had written it the way Mr. Jean-Louis had drilled them in September: if the array is sorted, don't crawl through it one element at a time like a linear search, checking every door on the street. Halve it. Look at the middle, decide which half your target must be in, throw the other half away, and do it again. Twenty comparisons instead of a million. She could say that in her sleep, and half the team still wrote the slow version anyway, which was why she'd been given the search in the first place.

The test data passed in three seconds. Then Zaid loaded the huge dataset, the one from last year's finals, and the program crashed. He leaned over her shoulder, read the midpoint line twice, and said, "There. You wrote low plus high divided by two." He tapped the screen. "On a dataset that size, low plus high is enormous. It overflows. Try low plus, in brackets, high minus low, all divided by two. Same middle, no overflow."

Brooke sat back. She remembered, suddenly and uncomfortably, the afternoon in the school library when she had watched Kayson lose a whole practice round to a bug he refused to show anyone, hunched over his keyboard, insisting he just needed one more minute, one more minute, until the timer ran out and he hadn't submitted anything at all. She had sworn then that she would never guard her code like that, that she'd let people read it early, and here she had nearly done the same thing by not asking anyone to look before the test run. She changed the line the way Zaid suggested, keeping the same low, the same high, the same division by two, just rearranged so nothing grew too large, and ran it again.

The huge dataset finished in under a second. Kayson peeled a clementine and divided it into thirds without being asked, which was his way of saying the afternoon had gone well. Their grandfather appeared at the doorway with a plate of sliced apples, surveyed the three of them bent over the laptop, and asked what exactly they were doing to his table.

"Searching," Brooke said. "A million numbers, and we only had to look at about twenty of them." He considered this, chewing, then said that in his day if you wanted to find something in a drawer you had to take the whole drawer apart, and that a virtuoso of any trade was simply someone who knew where not to look. He set down the plate and went back to his catalogs.

She wasn't sure the fixed line was beautiful. It was uglier than what she'd written, less like the clean proof from class, and she understood the shape of the problem it solved without being able to feel, in her hands, how a number could be too big for the box it lived in. But it ran, and it would run on anything the judges threw at it, and maybe that was the truer kind of elegance: the version that survives the world's actual size. She wrote the two forms side by side in her notebook and drew a box around the second one.

Zaid copied the fixed file onto his drive and started loading the next dataset. Outside, the light had gone orange on the fence posts. "Round two," he said, and hit enter.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Katherine stood at the picnic table at the edge of her grandmother's backyard, whisking oil into a bowl of egg yolk and lemon juice, and trying not to think about the fight. Her mother had said the words fiduciary like an accusation, as if honesty were a professional standard her father applied to clients but not to his own family, and Katherine had taken his side without meaning to. The dinner tonight was her idea of repairing it: her mother's favorite meal, made from scratch, potato salad and everything, in the backyard where the family had eaten every summer of Katherine's childhood.

The mayonnaise was the hard part. She added the oil slowly at first, a thin thread off the end of a spoon, and the mixture turned pale and thick and glossy, and she felt a small pride she hadn't earned yet. Then she got confident. She poured, the whisk lagged, and the whole thing went liquid and strange, oil pooling in a slick yellow lens on top of the water below it. She stared at it the way you stare at a machine that has quietly decided to stop being a machine.

Her grandmother came out with a plate of sliced tomatoes balanced on one arm and looked over her shoulder. "Broken," she said, not unkindly. "It happens to everyone once."

"It's ruined," Katherine said. "I'll just use the jar stuff."

"It's not ruined. Get me another yolk."

Katherine cracked an egg, separated it badly, cracked another, and her grandmother tipped the runny failure out of the bowl into a cup and put the fresh yolk in its place. "Now you add the broken one back in, slowly, like it's the oil. Whisk."

Katherine whisked. She added the split mixture a spoonful at a time, certain it wouldn't work, and then the yolk caught it, pulled it in, and the sauce came back together, thicker than before, smooth and hanging off the whisk in a slow ribbon. Behind them the grill ticked as it heated, and Willem, who had come over to help carry things and had so far only carried his phone to the lawn chair, called out, "Did you just perform witchcraft?"

"It's chemistry," Katherine said, mostly to see his face. He looked disappointed.

"Emulsifiers," her grandmother said, tapping the bowl with one finger. "In the yolk. Lecithin and the proteins."

Katherine pulled her phone out with a floury thumb and looked it up while the older woman sliced cucumbers beside her. It was true, and stranger than she'd expected: the lecithin and the proteins held tiny oil droplets suspended in the water so the sauce did not separate. She turned the bowl and watched it hold, one substance where a minute ago there had been two. It seemed almost malevolent of the first batch, the way it had split on her at the exact moment she'd trusted it, though she knew that was unfair. Oil and water simply wanted apart. Something had to stand between them and insist otherwise.

Willem wandered over, wiping lawn chair stripes off the back of his legs, and stood at her elbow. He had a way of showing up when things went wrong that she'd been grateful for since tenth grade, and had started, lately, to wonder about. "So your grandmother saved your potato salad," he said. "What are you saving?"

"Nothing. It's dinner."

"It's a peace offering," her grandmother said from the cucumber board, not looking up. "For her mother."

Willem raised his eyebrows and Katherine shook her head at him, small and quick, and he took the hint and went to check the grill nobody had asked him to check.

The twist came while she was folding the mayonnaise into the potatoes, still warm, the way the recipe said. Her grandmother sat down on the back step with her iced tea and said, almost to the tea, "You know that was never your mother's favorite. The potato salad." Katherine stopped folding. "She ate it every summer because I made it, and I made it because my mother made it. When she left for college she told me she'd been pretending for years. She thought I'd be hurt. I thought, good, she can finally tell me a true thing."

The potatoes were cooling. The table needed setting. Katherine stood there with the spoon in her hand, thinking that she had spent the whole afternoon trying to expiate an argument by cooking a meal built on a pretense, and that the mayonnaise had been more honest than any of them: it had split when it split, and it had come back together only when something stood in the middle and held the two things that wanted apart.

"So what do I do," she said, "if she hates it?"

Her grandmother shrugged, one shoulder, and sipped her tea. "Make it anyway. Ask her what she actually wants. She might even tell you."

The screen door banged and her mother came out into the backyard with a bottle of wine in each hand.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
Amy had read the help-wanted card so many times she could recite the phone number in her sleep, and on the morning of the interview she stood outside the coffee shop at quarter past nine, fifteen minutes early, rehearsing what she would say about herself to a manager she had never met. The window was still dark inside, chairs upturned on tables, and the crepuscular hush of the empty shop made her feel like a trespasser even on the sidewalk. She had one story prepared, the story of the group project that collapsed in her sophomore year, and she had no idea whether it would help her or sink her.

The night before, she had texted Genevieve, who had worked at a bakery all summer and therefore spoke with authority on the subject of interviews. "What do I even say when they ask about a time something went wrong," Amy wrote, thumb hovering. "I have the group project but it's kind of a disaster and I was sort of the one who dropped the ball."

Genevieve's reply came in three bubbles, the way her replies always did. "Ok so there's this thing my manager told me about. It's called the STAR method. You answer questions about past behavior by describing the Situation, then the Task you had, then the Action you took, then the Result." A second bubble: "It's not lying, it's structure." A third: "Even disasters have results."

Amy read it twice. It felt, on first pass, like a kind of artifice, a way of dressing up a mess in a blazer. But lying in bed, she turned it over and found she could not decide where the line fell between shaping a story and bending one. Both seemed possible. She fell asleep without deciding, which was, lately, how most of her questions got answered.

At nine twenty-five, a woman in a green apron unlocked the door and waved her in, and by ten past ten Amy was sitting across a small table from the manager, a clipboard between them, the espresso machine hissing behind the counter like a sleeping animal. "So," the manager said, "tell me about a time you worked with a team and it didn't go well."

Amy's mouth went dry, and then, unexpectedly, the structure was simply there, like a handrail on stairs she had climbed a hundred times in the dark. "The situation was a history project, four people, and two of them stopped showing up about a week in," she said. "The task was a twenty-minute presentation due Friday, and it was worth a third of our grade. The action I took was that I took the two missing parts, wrote them overnight, and emailed the other member, Aliya, to split the rehearsal. And the result was we got a B minus." She paused. "The result was also that I didn't sleep and I didn't tell the teacher, which I still don't know if I'd do again."

The manager looked up from the clipboard. "You know what, most people just say everything went fine and they learned teamwork."

"I did learn teamwork," Amy said. "I just learned it in the ugly version."

The manager laughed, a short surprised sound, and Amy felt something loosen in her chest. They talked through the register, the morning rush, the way regulars ordered the same thing for years and got wounded if you forgot. "Can you start Saturday?" the manager asked, and Amy said yes before she had finished deciding, because some answers arrive faster than the reasoning behind them.

Walking home, she called Genevieve. "I got it. I used your STAR thing and it actually worked."

"Told you," Genevieve said. "Situation, task, action, result. It works on college essays too, and on explaining to your mom why you're home late."

"It felt a little like cheating," Amy admitted. "Like I was performing my own life."

There was a pause on the line, the kind Genevieve used when she was choosing between comfort and honesty. "Maybe," she said finally. "But nobody wants the raw footage, Amy. Nobody has time."

On Saturday morning Amy arrived at six forty, before the sun had fully committed, and tied the apron strings behind her back twice because she got them wrong the first time. The manager handed her a rag and pointed at the tables by the window, and Amy began wiping them down in the gray light, the cloth squeaking against the wood, her phone silent in her pocket with two unread texts from the old group chat. At the third table she stopped, looked out at the empty street, and thought that she had told the story of the project a certain way yesterday and it had gotten her here, and that some part of the old messy version, the one where she had simply been scared, had stayed behind at that table across from the clipboard. She tucked the rag into her apron and went to learn the espresso machine.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen.
story:
Benjamin had been staring at the same curve for twenty minutes, and the curve, he felt, was staring back. It sat in his textbook like a smug cat, and beneath it, in the assignment's handwriting-copied font, sat the words: compute the area under this graph from zero to four. His mother had left a plate of toast at his elbow an hour ago. The toast had gone cold with solidarity.

"You're holding the pencil like it insulted your family," said Ahmed, who had let himself in through the back door the way he always did, and who was now raiding the fridge with the confidence of a second son. He dropped into the chair across the table and turned the textbook toward himself with two fingers, as if it might be contagious.

"It did insult my family. Look at it." Benjamin rotated the page. The curve swooped up, hesitated, swooped again. "The whole chapter keeps saying 'area under the curve' like that's supposed to mean something. Area of what? It's not a square. It's not a triangle. It's a shape with one side made of pure mood."

"That's why they invented the rectangles," Ahmed said around a wedge of cheese he had no right to. "Jasmine showed me this. You chop the region into skinny rectangles, add them up, then make them skinnier and skinnier until the sum stops changing. It's called the rectangle method."

"You're making that up."

"I'm facetious about many things, Benjamin, but not about rectangles."

Benjamin took out his phone and typed the method's name into the search bar, mostly to prove Ahmed wrong, partly because the toast was beyond saving and he needed a victory somewhere. The first result was not what he expected. It was a paragraph about a German mathematician, and he read it twice, the second time out loud, slowly, the way you read something when you suspect the universe of joking.

"Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen." He lowered the phone. "A job application. The man invented this in a job application. Like, 'here are my qualifications, also here is the entire foundation of calculus as you will know it, hire me.'"

"Imagine if you put that on your résumé," Ahmed said. " 'Skills: forks, Instagram, redefined the definite integral.' " He drew a rectangle on the margin of Benjamin's notebook, then a skinnier one inside it, then a skinnier one inside that, like a set of drawers. "There. Your mood-shape, tamed."

It was not tamed, exactly, but it was cornered. Benjamin sharpened his pencil with a violence the pencil had not earned and began. First he tried four rectangles, fat and clumsy, their tops jutting above the curve or sagging below it, and the sum came out to a number he wrote down with the solemn rectitude of a man signing a treaty he did not trust. Then eight rectangles. Then sixteen. He could feel what was happening before he could say it: the over-estimates and the under-estimates were closing in on each other, like hands reaching around a melon, and the number they were both creeping toward had a kind of patience to it. It had been sitting under that curve the whole time, waiting for him to bother.

"This is the strangest thing," he said. "I'm not finding the answer. The answer's already there. I'm just, like, sneaking up on it."

"That's very dramatic for a Tuesday."

"It is dramatic for a Tuesday." But he noticed that Ahmed had stopped eating the cheese and was watching the page, and that made him feel less alone with the weirdness of it. On one side there was the picture, the swooping cat-curve, a thing you could see and even feel in your wrist as you traced it. On the other side there was the list of numbers, the tidy sums marching toward something. And the whole trick, the entire invention Riemann had tucked into his lecturer application, was that both of those were the same object. The picture was the number. He could not fully believe that yet, and he said so.

"I mean, they never actually touch, right? The rectangles never become the curve. You just decide that close enough is close enough. Somebody had to decide that. Somebody had to say, this is where we stop, this is the area now."

"That's the most suspicious thing about math," Ahmed agreed. "It works, and nobody apologizes for it."

The doorbell rang, which was odd, because nobody who rang the doorbell ever came to the kitchen, and yet Ms. Hernández from across the street was suddenly in the doorway holding a casserole dish and looking over Benjamin's shoulder at the notebook before anyone had said hello.

"Sixteen rectangles," she said. "Bold. Riemann himself would have used infinitely many, and he still had to apply twice."

Benjamin looked up. "Twice?"

She set the casserole down next to the cold toast and smiled at the page. "Hand me that pencil, and I'll show you where your fourth rectangle is lying to you."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
story:
The credit union smelled like carpet cleaner and warm paper, and Kevin stood in front of the rate board the way other people stood in front of aquariums. Two numbers hung above the savings row, 4.65 percent and 4.75 percent, and beneath them, in smaller type, the words "compounded monthly." He had walked in intending to ask about a loan, but the two percentages had stopped him, because they seemed to describe the same account, and he could not understand why the same money would grow at two different speeds.

He had nine hundred dollars to borrow, not save. The Corolla's transmission had begun to make a sound like a spoon in a garbage disposal, and without the car he could not get to the warehouse job he was supposed to start Monday, which would incapacitate the whole plan: the job paid for the car, the car got him to the job. He was seventeen, which meant every adult at this counter could tell him no on principle, and the loan would technically be in his mother's name, a fact he had not fully explained to her yet, or to himself.

A voice beside him said, "You're doing the face." Vanessa had followed him in from the parking lot, ostensibly to deposit a birthday check, mostly because she was bored. She followed his eyes to the board. "Which one's the real one?"

"They both are, apparently. Same account." He took a brochure from the rack, and there it was again in print, 4.65 percent compounded monthly, 4.75 percent APY. He read the line twice. "That can't be a typo twice."

"That's the APY," Vanessa said, pointing at the larger number. "Annual percentage yield." She said it the way she said the names of bands, as if he should already know.

"Which is different from the rate." He turned the brochure over, looking for fine print that would contradict her, and found none. So the two numbers were not competing claims about the same thing; they were the same thing measured differently, one of them folded to include what happened when the growth itself started growing. The smaller number was the honest month-by-month speed. The bigger number was what you actually ended the year with. He felt the small, specific satisfaction of a door opening in a wall he had assumed was impermeable.

At the counter, the loan officer was a patient man named Mr. Lombardi, who did not lecture, which Kevin appreciated, having braced himself for pedantry. Mr. Lombardi turned the monitor toward him instead and let Kevin read the loan terms himself: the amount, the term, and an APR that Kevin now understood was a cousin of the number on the board, working in the opposite direction, a percentage that would make the borrowed nine hundred cost more the longer he took to give it back. "So the bank's rate makes my savings grow," Kevin said slowly, "and the same kind of number makes what I owe grow." Mr. Lombardi said only, "That's the shape of it," and slid the signature page across.

Kevin did not sign it. He asked for a day, and outside, in the lot, he told Vanessa the part he had not told anyone: the Corolla was his mother's car, and the new job was in the opposite direction from her clinic, and the plan was to drive her to her appointments before his shift and still somehow make both. He had framed it, in his own head, as simple arithmetic. Hearing it out loud, it sounded like a machine with too few belts. Vanessa said nothing for a moment, which from her was loud.

That night there was a message on his phone from Gabrielle, who had moved to Phoenix in March and still wrote in full sentences like a person from another century. "My dad did this thing when our car died," she wrote. "He sat with the numbers for a week and everyone called it stalling, but he said the week was the cheapest thing he ever bought, because the first offer was never the only offer. Also: credit unions are not banks and they know it, so make them act like it. Ask what happens if you pay it back early. G." Kevin read it three times, then opened the loan officer's printout again and looked for the prepayment line, and found a word there, "penalty," struck through by hand with initials beside it, which meant someone at this branch had already removed it, quietly, before he even asked.

He did not know yet whether the schedule would hold, whether he could carry his mother's mornings and his own evenings in the same borrowed car, whether nine hundred would be enough or only the beginning of what the transmission wanted. What he had, going back through the doors the next afternoon with the papers in his hand, was the two numbers and the one week and the sense, new to him, that money was not a fixed thing but a slope, and that slopes ran in both directions. He set the pages on the counter in front of Mr. Lombardi and said, "Same terms. And I want the first payment to be bigger than the rest."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java fields left uninitialized get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, and null for object references.
story:
Michael had named the class Dog, which felt absurd until it didn't, the way most things in Mr. Zhou's computer science course felt absurd until they suddenly worked. The assignment was to build a Java class with private fields, getter methods, and a test that proved everything ran, and Michael had stayed after the final bell because the lab was warm and his house was not, and because the screen gave him something to argue with that argued back.

He typed the fields first: private String name; private int age; private boolean vaccinated; Then a constructor, then get methods, one for each. Somewhere behind him, Linda and Anouk were arguing about whether a getter should be called getName or fetchName, a debate Michael privately considered beneath both of them, though he said nothing, because Linda had a way of lionizing whichever convention she'd read about most recently, and contradicting her was rarely worth the hour it cost.

He remembered the first week of the term, before any of this made sense, when Mr. Zhou had put a broken program on the projector and let the whole class stare at it in silence for eleven minutes. Michael had counted. Nobody had raised a hand. He'd had a presentiment then, vague and cold, that this course was going to be less about computers than about how long he could stand not knowing something, and the presentiment had turned out to be accurate, though not in the way he'd feared.

Now he wrote his test: create a Dog, print its name, check its age. He ran it before finishing the constructor, just to see. The console printed null. Not an error, not a blank, but the word itself, sitting there like a small verdict. Michael sat back. He had expected the program to complain, to refuse, the way a person refuses when you ask them a question they can't answer. Instead it answered, calmly, with null.

"Yours printed null too?" Anouk had drifted over, chair wheels squeaking against the linoleum. He was mercurial about these things, careless for an hour and then seized by a problem, and this was clearly a seized hour.

"Mine printed null and a zero," Michael said. "And it printed false."

"For real? You didn't set anything?"

"I set name. I think. Let me look." He scrolled up and found it: in the constructor he had typed the parameter, and then assigned the parameter to itself, a perfect little circle going nowhere. So the field never got the value. But that explained null. It did not explain the zero, or the false, because those were fields he had never touched at all, and yet there they were, printed, definite.

Anouk leaned in. "So wait. It prints false even though you never said anything about vaccinated?"

"That's the part I don't get. It's like the fields already had values before I did anything."

Linda rolled her chair over from the other side of the lab, drawn by the smell of confusion, which was the only thing that reliably drew her. "Show me." She read the screen for a moment, chewing the end of a pen cap. "Try one more," she said. "Make a field that's a String, another object type, and don't set it either."

"There aren't any other," Michael started to say, and then made one: private Dog mother; He printed mother and got null again, exactly like the name. Numbers got zero, booleans got false, and object things like Strings and Dogs got null, whether he wanted them to or not. It was almost tidy, the way the language quietly filled in defaults rather than failing, though he wasn't sure yet whether quiet defaults were a kindness or a trap. A program that lied to you loudly was one thing. A program that handed you a calm zero could hide a mistake for weeks.

He fixed the constructor, ran the test, and watched the real name appear where null had been. Anouk clapped once, the way people clap at a tennis match, and Linda wrote something in her notebook, which was how she claimed territory. Michael saved the file and then, before closing it, added one more test on purpose: a Dog with nothing set at all, printing everything, the zero and the false and the null lined up in the console like exhibits.

"Why that one?" Linda asked.

"So I remember," Michael said. "The test I fail on purpose is the one that teaches me the most." He wasn't entirely sure that was true, or true always, or true for anyone but him, but he hit run again anyway, and the three defaults printed one more time, patient and blank, waiting for whoever forgot next.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
Daniel had the kitchen table to himself until six, which was the whole plan: a painting for his grandmother's eightieth, the harbor at Chittagong where she'd grown up, worked from a photograph he'd taken the summer he was fifteen, the last summer she told stories at that table. He'd promised her something framed. He had two weeks, and tonight was for the sky at dawn, which in the photograph was a rose-gold he could almost name but not quite reproduce.

He laid out his acrylics in a row, squeezed a coin of each color onto a paper plate, and began with white and red, thinning the red until the pink was close. Then gold. Then, when the gold wasn't warm enough, a touch of orange, and then, because the orange pulled it toward traffic cone, a thread of blue to cool it back. He leaned toward the photograph taped to the cupboard door. The mixture on his brush had gone the color of an old brick.

He kept going, because that was what he'd always done. In fifth grade he'd learned that stubbornness could pass for talent, that teachers rewarded the kid who stayed at the easel while everyone else went to lunch. He added white to lift it. The white barely moved it. He added yellow, then red again, then more white, and the pile on the plate darkened by degrees into something like wet cardboard, its surface glossless, its color an accusation.

The door opened and Camron came in with Baby behind him, both of them smelling of the pool at the community center, towels around their necks like scarves. "You said you'd come," Camron said, but without heat, and dropped into the chair across from the ruined palette.

"I said I might." Daniel gestured at the plate. "Tell me what that is."

Baby leaned over it, arms folded on the table. "Dirt," she said. "Or chili. Cold chili."

"It was pink an hour ago." He pushed the plate toward them like evidence. "Every color I liked, I put in. It should be brighter than any of them. Instead it's this."

Baby picked up his palette knife, held it to the light, set it down. "Paint's not light," she said. "My physics teacher kept going on about this. Each pigment absorbs part of the light, so the more pigments you mix in, the more light gets absorbed, and it all tends toward a dark, muddy color instead of white. She called it subtractive. That's why your pile looks like dirt."

"Subtractive," Daniel repeated. He looked at the photograph, then at the plate, then at the photograph. Somewhere in his head, two ideas that had lived separately folded into each other: that paint was stuff, not brightness, and that adding was not the same as increasing. It was inchoate, the thought, still more feeling than formulation, but it had a shape now.

He wet a rag and wiped the plate clean, and Camron, who had watched all this with the acumen of a boy who fixed engines and distrusted shortcuts, interposed a hand over the clean plate before Daniel could start again. "So don't mix six things," Camron said. "Mix two. Get the rose right first, flat, then put the gold on top of it thin, so both show."

From the hallway came a knock, and Mr. Chowdhury from next door stood at the screen with a bowl of something in his hands, drawn by the lights and the noise the way he always was at dinnertime. He looked at the photograph on the cupboard, at the wet canvas with its one honest stripe of flat rose, and said nothing for a moment, and Daniel found he wanted the man's approval more than he'd wanted the perfect color an hour before, though he couldn't have said why, and didn't try.

He loaded the brush with rose, unmixed, and carried it to the canvas.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Chicago style offers two citation systems: notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and author-date, common in the sciences.
story:
Mr. Oliveira handed back the essay with a red circle around the third page and one word in the margin: system. Jason read it twice in the aisle between the study tables before he sat down. He had written the paper for history on the Marshall Plan, fourteen sources, and he had put the citations in parentheses after each quote, the way his chemistry teacher wanted last semester. At the bottom of the last page Mr. Oliveira had written a fuller note: Chicago style, wrong one.

He spread the marked pages across the table under the window. Ronald leaned over from the next seat, chewing the cap of a pen. "What'd you get?"

"Nothing yet. He didn't grade it. I used the wrong citations."

Ronald picked up page three and squinted at it. "Citations are citations."

"That's what I thought." Jason opened his laptop and typed Chicago style into the catalogue search, then gave up on the catalogue and used the general terminal by the reference desk. The library's copy of the style manual was on the shelf behind the desk, spine faded, dust along the top edge. He carried it back with both hands because it was the size of a paving stone.

Douglas arrived twenty minutes later with a bag of chips he wasn't supposed to have indoors and pulled a chair up backwards. "Are those footnotes? You wrote footnotes?"

"I'm learning to." Jason turned to the tabbed section and found the page. The manual laid out two options, and he read them slowly, once to himself and once out loud in a low voice so Ronald and Douglas could hear. "Notes and bibliography, that's the one for history and the humanities. Author-date is for the sciences. There are two systems, and they don't mix."

"So you did the science one," Douglas said.

"I did the science one in a history class." It sounded worse said aloud. The moribund feeling of the returned paper, the thing he'd thought finished, was back open in front of him, all fourteen sources needing to be rehung.

He started converting. The parenthetical citations came out and superscript numbers went in, and at the bottom of each page he built the notes, one at a time, checking the model in the manual for where the period went after the title instead of before it. Ronald watched over his shoulder for a while, then went back to his own homework. Douglas ate the chips in the stairwell where the cameras didn't reach and came back smelling of salt.

Halfway through, Jason stopped. The reason he had used author-date was not laziness. He had liked it. It was clean, it kept the argument visible, it said its piece in parentheses and got out of the way. The notes and bibliography system put the evidence down at the bottom of the page like a conversation under the conversation, and he had assumed that was clutter. But sitting here with the manual open, he could see the other case: in history, the sources were part of the thinking, and the footnotes let a reader follow the thinking down. He wasn't sure he fully believed that. Maybe both were defensible and the choice was mostly a convention of the field, a handshake everyone agreed to. He wrote both possibilities in the margin of his notebook, then crossed out neither.

At four o'clock the light through the window went long and orange across the tables, which seemed to presage the security guard's walk-through and the announcement that the library closed at five on Saturdays. Mr. Oliveira came by on his rounds, saw the manual open to the tabbed section, and paused.

"You found it," he said.

"There are two of them," Jason said. "I didn't know that."

Mr. Oliveira tapped the cover once and moved on toward the front desk without another word. Douglas leaned over and read the last footnote Jason had typed, then scrolled down to the bibliography taking shape on its own page.

"That's like a whole second paper," Douglas said.

"It's the same paper," Jason said. He typed the final entry, checked the hanging indent against the model, and hit print. The printer at the reference desk ground awake after a moment of silence. Jason stood and walked toward it, and Ronald, without looking up from his homework, said, "Bring back the good pages."
